articles.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on  The GuardianTrump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going  BBCTrump: Zelensky never wanted to end Ukraine war  The TelegraphRussian strikes ‘leave half a million Ukrainian homes without power’  The TimesTrump says Zelenskiy should get somebody else to negotiate to end war  Reuters
articles.full_text:
- Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.
- Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones.
- Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”
- In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage. In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.
- Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed, a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced the controversial agreement with Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”
- Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- Russia’s defence ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a “massive strike” on targets in Kyiv and the Ukraine’s capital region. The ministry said the attack targeted military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones and data centres. Earlier, Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said a Russian air strike had killed one person and injured two in the city overnight. A medical facility and a non-residential building were damaged in the attack, he said.
- A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday, officials said. Ukraine’s foreign ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.

Oil prices have reversed higher in light of fresh reports about two separate Middle East strikes. WTI had traded down to $99.24 earlier and brent to $106.82, both after the US waived santions on Russian fuel.
That move now seems to have bought about 15 hours of lower oil prices and now crude is up on the day, with WTI at $103.13 and brent just above $110.
Two stories have driven the gains, the first is that the Iranian navy said the US attacked the Konarek naval base with "two light projectiles" early this morning and that wo solidiers were injured.
More recently, a pair of reports highlight that Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia in the past 48 hours, including strikes on the Yanbu oil facility owned by Aramco, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Ryiadh and Abha. Today, Saudi Arabia cancelled this year's 'Davos in the Desert' conference.
The next quesion is what will be the retaliation for the latest strikes on both sides. The US hadn't attacked Iran in seven weeks; Trump also said no attacks before the midterms. This one was characterized as small so perhaps it's ignored as Iran continues to focus on striking ships transiting Hormuz.
WTI crude oil daily:
Looking at the chart, oil has been climbing steadily higher in the past two weeks and is now within striking distance of the Sept 14 high of $104.95. We're getting very close to the point where a drop is too late to help Trump in the midterms so negotiations will be fruitless, despite a Qatari report today about new proposals.
Beyond the midterms, the calculus likely points to escalation, though at that point Republicans and Democrats may wish to sharpen their anti-war chops ahead of the 2028 election cycle. If Republicans suffer a rough defeat in the midterms, Congress could add pressure on Trump to exit Iran and find a way to make a deal. Alternatively, the US administration may simply conclude that the blockade on Iran and periodic strikes on shipping is a long-term strategy that will win.
What's more-concerning than the near-term chart is that if you look further out on the curve. October 2027 oil prices are at $83 and that's up $13 since the start of September and above the pre-war peak. That's the market doubting the endless promises from Trump that oil prices will "come crashing down".

articles.title: Indian Refiners’ Russian Crude Trade Exposes EU Sanctions Gap - Urban Acres
articles.summary: Indian Refiners’ Russian Crude Trade Exposes EU Sanctions Gap  Urban Acres
articles.full_text:
The figures point to a complex re-routing of energy trade rather than a simple rise in Indian crude consumption. India’s Russian crude imports fell 13 per cent in September, yet refineries operating with Russian feedstock continued to send substantial volumes of fuel to markets in the European Union, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. The central question is therefore not only how much Russian crude India buys, but how sanctions treat products after that crude has passed through a refinery.
The distinction matters because refining transforms the physical product while leaving the commercial and regulatory question of origin contested. The European Union banned imports of oil products refined from Russian crude in January 2026. However, the ban exempts net crude exporters. CREA argues that this exemption leaves a gap because a country’s net-exporter status does not prevent individual refineries within that country from processing Russian-origin crude.
The report recommends applying the restriction at the refinery level. Under that approach, oil products from any plant that had processed Russian crude during the previous six months would be barred, regardless of the declared origin of the specific cargo. This is a recommendation from an advocacy group, not an adopted policy, but it identifies the administrative problem at the heart of the trade: the difficulty of linking a finished fuel cargo to the crude feedstock used months earlier.
India’s refinery network sits at the centre of this issue. Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat supplied six of the seven cargoes unloaded at European Union ports in September, CREA said. The refinery also supplied the group’s largest United States-bound exports, valued at 122 million euros. Russian crude accounted for 32 per cent of Jamnagar’s imports between July and September.
The EU received oil products worth 667 million euros from refineries in India, Turkiye and Brunei that process Russian crude. Australia received products worth 168 million euros, the United States 154 million euros and New Zealand 19 million euros. For the EU-bound shipments, Italy received three of the seven cargoes, Romania received two, and Spain and Cyprus received one each.
The value of exports destined for EU ports from refineries running on Russian crude rose 80 per cent, according to CREA. That figure included a 104,000-tonne gasoil cargo from Jamnagar that was still travelling to Rotterdam. The cargo illustrates the way sanctions enforcement must operate across multiple points: the refinery, the shipping route, the declared destination and the rules governing the receiving market.
At the same time, the volume of Russian crude entering India declined. CREA said imports fell for the second consecutive month and reached their lowest level since April. Intake dropped at India’s three largest Russian-crude-importing refineries: Jamnagar by 27 per cent, Indian Oil Corporation’s Paradip refinery by 21 per cent and Nayara Energy’s Vadinar refinery by 8 per cent.
Vadinar nevertheless overtook Jamnagar as India’s largest importer of Russian crude in September. The change shows why monthly national import figures do not fully explain how the market is being reorganised. A decline in total imports can coexist with shifts between individual facilities, changing cargo flows and continued exports of refined products to sanctioning countries.
Smaller installations also mostly reduced their intake. The HMEL Mundra Oil Terminal cut imports by 74 per cent month on month, while the Kochi refinery reduced them by 32 per cent. The main exception was Indian Oil Corporation’s Mundra Oil Terminal, which received 570,000 tonnes of Russian crude in September after receiving none in August.
India remained Russia’s second-largest fossil-fuel customer in September, buying 4.1 billion euros of Russian hydrocarbons, CREA said. Crude oil accounted for 88 per cent of that total, at 3.6 billion euros. Coal accounted for 309 million euros and oil products for 161 million euros. Only China bought more Russian fossil fuels during the month.
Since December 2022, India has taken 37 per cent of Russia’s crude exports, compared with China’s 50 per cent, according to the report. Before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India was a marginal buyer of Russian oil. Its position changed after Western buyers retreated and Russian crude became available at steep discounts.
The price difference remains an important part of the trade’s economics. Urals crude averaged 90.7 US dollars a barrel in September but remained 23 dollars below Brent, unchanged from August. The discount creates an incentive for refiners to continue assessing Russian crude as part of their feedstock mix, even as the compliance environment becomes more restrictive in some markets.
Kpler analysts attributed part of the September fall in Indian volumes to tighter supply and stronger Chinese competition for Russian barrels, rather than only to pressure from the United States. They expect India’s October imports to remain between 1.8 million and 1.9 million barrels per day. That estimate, as reported in the source material, indicates that India’s role in the trade is not disappearing even if the composition and distribution of imports are changing.
The institutional challenge is that sanctions are being applied to a supply chain that is organised across jurisdictions. Russian crude may be purchased by an Indian refinery, converted into diesel or another petroleum product, and shipped to a market where imports of products made from Russian crude are restricted. Each transaction can have a different legal and commercial identity, while the physical transformation makes the original feedstock less visible in the final cargo.
That creates a governance problem for regulators and customs authorities. A rule based only on the declared origin of a finished product may not capture the origin of the crude used to make it. A refinery-level rule, such as the one proposed by CREA, would make the plant’s recent processing history a central compliance factor. It could also make enforcement more administratively demanding because authorities would need reliable records of crude intake and a defined look-back period.
The available evidence does not establish that the EU or other sanctioning countries have adopted CREA’s recommendation. Nor does it show that any specific cargo breached a final legal determination. What it does establish is a sharp increase in the value of oil products shipped by refineries processing Russian crude, alongside continued imports of Russian hydrocarbons by India and a policy debate over how refined-product restrictions should be enforced.
For Indian cities and the wider built environment, the issue is indirect but important. Refineries are major industrial infrastructure nodes whose operations connect ports, storage terminals, pipelines, shipping routes, manufacturing activity and public revenues. Changes in the source and price of crude can affect how these assets are used, while changes in sanctions rules can alter cargo destinations and the commercial value of refinery capacity.
The September data also show why energy infrastructure cannot be understood only through national import totals. Jamnagar, Vadinar, Paradip, Mundra and Kochi recorded different movements in Russian-crude intake. Those facility-level changes shape port utilisation, tanker movements, storage demand and the export profile of refined products. The distribution of activity across refineries is therefore as significant as the headline decline in India’s total imports.
The evidence points to a market balancing three forces: discounted Russian supply, competition from China for available barrels and growing scrutiny from sanctioning countries. India’s crude imports from Russia declined in September, but the country remained the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels and Indian refineries continued to supply major Western markets.
The next stage of the story will depend on whether sanctioning jurisdictions retain country-level exemptions or move towards refinery-level restrictions. It will also depend on how Indian refiners adjust their crude mix, how Russian supplies are allocated between Indian and Chinese buyers, and whether October imports remain within the 1.8 million-to-1.9 million barrels-per-day range cited by Kpler analysts. The immediate evidence confirms a continuing trade relationship; the unresolved issue is how effectively existing rules can follow crude through the refinery and into the final fuel market.

articles.title: UK publishes CBAM default emissions values ahead of 2027 launch - edie
articles.summary: UK publishes CBAM default emissions values ahead of 2027 launch  edie
articles.full_text:
Published by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) today (19 October), the values cover aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel.
The mechanism is intended to address carbon leakage, which occurs when production moves to countries with weaker climate policies or lower carbon costs.
UK CBAM will apply to imports of covered goods, with the tax calculated by reference to the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions generated during their production, subject to relevant carbon pricing adjustments.
The Emissions and Verification Regulations establish how embodied emissions must be calculated, how the underlying data must be monitored and verified, and which records businesses must retain.
Importers can use one of two methods to calculate emissions. The first is to apply the published default value for the relevant CBAM good. The calculation involves multiplying the weight of the imported goods by the applicable emissions value, without requiring independent verification of the emissions figure.
The alternative is to use actual emissions data from the installation where the goods were manufactured or processed. This method requires more detailed information and independent verification by accredited third-party verifiers, but may result in a lower calculated emissions figure and, consequently, a lower tax liability.
Importers bringing in less than £10,000 worth of covered CBAM goods over a 12-month period are exempt from registration and reporting obligations.
Transitional period to allow accounting flexibility
The UK CBAM is scheduled to begin on 1 January 2027. A transitional period will run from 1 January 2027 to 30 June 2028, allowing businesses flexibility around accounting periods and initial payments before full quarterly reporting and tax liabilities take effect.
The launch will coincide with the second allocation phase of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS), covering 2027 to 2030. During this period, free emissions allowances for domestic producers will be phased out over several years, with the aim of maintaining parity between UK production and imports subject to CBAM.
Six-year record-keeping requirement
HMRC has also published guidance on the records businesses must retain under the mechanism.
CBAM records must be kept in written form, including electronically, for six years from the later of the date the records were created or the end of the accounting period to which they relate.
Businesses that fail to retain the required records may face a fixed penalty of £500. Separate penalties may apply if an importer fails to provide information or documents when requested by HMRC.
The requirements mean importers will need to maintain records supporting their emissions calculations and compliance with the scheme, whether they use default values or actual emissions data.
The UK mechanism follows the same broad approach as the EU’s CBAM, although the UK is developing its own rules and administrative requirements.
The EU’s definitive CBAM phase began in 2026, increasing the focus on carbon costs across international industrial supply chains.
The UK scheme’s introduction in 2027 will add another set of carbon reporting and tax requirements for businesses importing covered industrial goods into the country.

- HMRC has published default emissions values for goods covered by the UK’s incoming Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
- The figures provide an alternative when verified emissions data is unavailable.
- The import levy is scheduled to begin on January 1, 2027, covering five industrial sectors.
The UK has published default emissions values for its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), giving importers a new reference point for calculating potential carbon tax liabilities before the scheme begins in 2027. HM Revenue & Customs released the figures on October 16, alongside guidance on how businesses should use them.
The benchmarks cover selected products in the aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel sectors. Importers can use the published values in CBAM returns instead of verified actual emissions data, according to the government guidance.
In a written statement to Parliament, the Treasury also outlined the next steps for implementing the scheme, including how the emissions figures will feed into the calculation of importers’ liabilities.
A new cost for carbon-intensive imports
The UK CBAM is due to take effect on January 1, 2027. It is designed to address carbon leakage, the risk that production shifts to countries with weaker climate policies or lower carbon costs. The charge will reflect emissions associated with covered goods, alongside relevant carbon pricing adjustments.
The system follows a similar broad approach to the European Union’s carbon border mechanism, although the UK is developing its own rules. The EU’s definitive CBAM phase began in 2026, increasing the focus on carbon costs across international industrial supply chains.
Businesses prepare for implementation
For importers, the new defaults offer a practical way to estimate emissions where verified product-specific data is not available. Businesses will still need to understand which goods fall within scope and how the applicable rules affect their reporting and tax calculations.
The publication marks another step toward the UK’s new carbon pricing regime. Importers and suppliers are likely to focus increasingly on emissions documentation, sourcing decisions and the potential financial impact of the scheme as its start date approaches.

articles.title: The EU AI Act and UK AI regulation: A product law perspective - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.summary: The EU AI Act and UK AI regulation: A product law perspective  Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.full_text:
Don't just teach AI, use it
Regulation EU 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act) is widely regarded as a landmark piece of legislation. It introduces a dedicated legal framework for artificial intelligence (AI), adopts a risk-based approach to regulation, and places fundamental rights considerations at the heart of compliance.
While the EU has adopted a dedicated legislative framework for AI, the UK has, to date, favoured a more principles-based and sector-led approach, relying largely on existing regulatory frameworks. At first glance, that divergence may suggest that the compliance challenges facing businesses operating in the EU and UK are materially different.
For product lawyers, however, many of the concepts underpinning the EU AI Act are not entirely new. Many of its operational requirements, including risk management, post-market monitoring, incident investigation, regulatory notification, and corrective action, reflect concepts that have long featured in product regulation.
For decades, EU product laws have required manufacturers and other economic operators to monitor products through their lifecycle, assess risks, and take appropriate action where issues emerge. Viewed through that lens, many of the EU AI Act's operational requirements, which appear to borrow directly from the product safety playbook, will be familiar to organisations accustomed to product regulatory compliance.
A familiar approach to managing risk
One of the clearest parallels is that compliance obligations do not simply end once a product or system reaches the market.
Under EU product legislation, manufacturers are expected to continue monitoring products, gather information about real-world performance and respond when risks emerge. Increasingly, EU product regulation is built around lifecycle compliance rather than a one-off assessment undertaken before a product is placed on the market. This broader shift towards lifecycle regulation will be familiar to many businesses operating across both EU and UK product regulatory landscapes.
The EU AI Act adopts a similar philosophy. Providers of high-risk AI systems must establish post-market monitoring systems, collect information about the operation of their systems in practice and assess whether risks, incidents or non-conformities emerge after deployment. The objective is not simply to demonstrate compliance before a system reaches the market, but to continually assess whether that system continues to operate as intended.
Responding to risks and non-compliance
The similarities become even clearer when issues arise after products or systems have been placed on the market.
Under Regulation (EU) 2023/988 (the EU General Product Safety Regulation or EU GPSR), a manufacturer that considers, or has reason to believe, that a product is dangerous must act immediately. Depending on the circumstances, this may involve taking corrective measures, including withdrawal, or recall. Authorities must be notified and, where a recall is undertaken, consumers may also need to be informed.
Similar concepts can be found across the broader EU product regulatory framework. For example, under Directive 2011/65/EU (the Restriction on Hazardous Materials Directive or RoHS Directive), manufacturers that consider, or have reason to believe, that an in-scope product is non-compliant must take corrective measures and notify competent authorities.
The EU AI Act adopts both of these approaches:
- Where a provider considers, or has reason to believe, that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity, it must immediately take the necessary corrective action, which may involve bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it.
- Where a provider becomes aware that a high-risk AI system presents a risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights, it must immediately investigate the causes of the risk and inform market surveillance authorities (and, where applicable, the notified body) of the nature of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken.
Incident reporting: product safety thinking applied to AI
The parallels become even more apparent in the EU AI Act's serious incident reporting regime.
Providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to market surveillance authorities. Reports must generally be submitted immediately after the provider establishes, or reasonably suspects, a causal link between the AI system and the incident, and, in any event, no later than 15 days after becoming aware of the incident.
The regime also includes accelerated reporting deadlines in particularly serious circumstances:
- Widespread infringements, or incidents involving serious and irreversible disruption to critical infrastructure, must be reported immediately, and no later than 2 days after the provider (or deployer) becomes aware of that incident.
- Incidents involving death must be reported immediately after a causal relationship is established or suspected and, in any event, no later than 10 days after the provider (or deployer) becomes aware of the incident.
Reporting is only one element of the process. Following the report, providers of high-risk AI systems must also investigate the incident, conduct a risk assessment, cooperate with authorities, and implement any necessary corrective measures.
For organisations with established product safety procedures, many of these requirements will already be well understood. The practical questions are often the same: what happened, is there a causal link, how serious is the risk, does the regulator need to be informed and what corrective action is required?
Although these are classic product safety questions, they are increasingly becoming AI governance questions.
Fundamental rights: the key differentiator
However, there is one important difference.
Traditionally, product safety law has focused on protecting consumers against physical harms such as injury, death, or property damage.
The EU AI Act adopts a broader concept of risk. A serious incident may involve not only health and safety impacts, but also infringements of fundamental rights protected under EU law. For example, risks relating to discrimination, privacy, or freedom of expression may arise even where no physical harm occurs.
In that sense, the EU AI Act expands the categories of harms that must be monitored and managed. This means that, while many of the governance mechanisms found in the EU AI Act resemble those found elsewhere in product regulation, the nature of the risks that need to be assessed is considerably broader.
What about the UK?
Although the UK has not adopted legislation equivalent to the EU AI Act, many of the same governance themes are beginning to emerge through existing regulatory frameworks and guidance. AI-related risks are increasingly being considered through the lens of established product safety, consumer protection, data protection and sector-specific regulation.
For example, organisations developing or deploying AI systems may already need to address AI-related risks under existing UK data protection requirements, while AI-enabled products remain subject to established product safety obligations.
For businesses operating across both jurisdictions, the EU AI Act may therefore have an influence extending beyond those activities that fall directly within its scope. The practical disciplines that it requires, including risk assessment, incident escalation, monitoring and governance, are likely to shape wider organisational practices, even where equivalent legal obligations do not currently exist under a standalone UK AI regime.
What does this mean for businesses?
The practical implication is that compliance with the EU AI Act may not require an entirely new approach to governance.
Many businesses already have established processes for monitoring products, investigating issues and engaging with regulators. For those organisations, the challenge may be less about building entirely new compliance structures and more about adapting existing governance frameworks to address AI-specific risks, including risks relating to fundamental rights.
This may be particularly true for businesses operating across both the UK and EU. Even where organisations are not subject to an equivalent standalone AI regime in the UK, compliance with the EU AI Act may influence governance standards across wider business operations.
Ultimately, while the EU AI Act introduces a novel regulatory framework for AI, businesses that already understand post-market monitoring, incident reporting, corrective action and regulatory engagement may be better placed than they expect to respond to its requirements. The challenge is likely to lie not in the underlying governance disciplines themselves, but in applying them to a new category of risks, including those relating to fundamental rights.
Authored by Valerie Kenyon, Eshana Subherwal, Vicki Kooner, and Magdalena Bakowska.

articles.title: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe's streets ablaze - News4JAX
articles.summary: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe's streets ablaze  News4JAX
articles.full_text:
MADRID – Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.
Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.
Recommended Videos
Young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”
Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in NATO countries.
Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing on his Truth Social platform: “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” on Monday.
Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other elements including black-clad, masked agitators have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants.
Here's a look at what's driving the unrest:
Students say education resources are dwindling
In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they call understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.
The protests then broadened as France's CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.
Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.
In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.
Unaffordable housing stymies young people
In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.
The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, triggering a snap election announced by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez for November. A general strike also was called for November — the first in 14 years.
Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges.
Spain's minimum wage is 1,221 euros ($1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about $1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión.
“Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do,” said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. “This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city.”
Untenable living costs as inflation rises in Italy
“Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education, and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2% in September, surpassing the eurozone’s 3.8%, according to government data.
The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna, and in Italy's finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested — most of them minors — and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the “Oct. 17 Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.
Students in Albania join anti-corruption protests
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants in the United States, where President Donald Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.
In Serbia, the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections.
The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the Oct. 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fueling fears of possible violence.

articles.summary: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals  The GuardianUK steelmakers pay 49% more for electricity than French rivals  Engineering and Technology MagazineBritish steelmakers face ‘severe disadvantage’ due to UK electricity prices  Project ScotlandElectricity costs will put pressure on British steel in 2026  InspenetGap with France in electricity prices for steelmakers reaches £30 per MWh — The Guardian &nb...
articles.full_text:
British steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.
The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.
Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to his goal of “reindustrialising” the UK.
Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial for cleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces.
The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas price determines the price of electricity even from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has caused global gas prices to soar.
Electricity prices in France are mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.
Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.
The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.
Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.
The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group has proposed a cap on prices that it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.
“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.
“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”
Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.
Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.
A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”

articles.title: What my kettle tells us about Chinese car tariffs - The Telegraph
articles.summary: What my kettle tells us about Chinese car tariffs  The TelegraphFrance drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation  The GuardianFrance and Germany to allow UK to join EU car policy if it aligns on China tariffs  Financial TimesChina warns UK against following EU on EV restrictions, vows retaliation  CnEVPostBeware ‘Trojan Horse’ tactics by Chinese car producers  The Herald
articles.full_text:
This will be a “cost of living government”, the Prime Minister has declared. Also Andy Burnham: it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to move closer to the EU.
Very soon, he will have to make a choice (not the PM’s strongest point). The EU demands that if the UK is to join its “Made in Europe” subsidy and trade preference scheme to counter Chinese imports, we must follow Brussels in imposing tariffs of 45 per cent on Chinese cars. That would amount to a new tax on British consumers and almost certainly lead to higher prices on all new cars here (as other producers would take advantage of the diminution of competition).
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, seems opposed to the idea, warning that China would retaliate against UK exporters (“if you put trade protection up, they’ll probably be reciprocated and you’ll lose out”). Similar arguments were put by Matthew Lynn in these pages, in a column headlined “There’s nothing wrong with buying Chinese cars”. That seemed to enrage readers, many of whom made reasonable points about the callous nature of the regime in Beijing, its behaviour over Hong Kong, and its push for trade supremacy. Yet anyone of such opinions – and I share them – is not obliged to buy a Chinese car.
Though I wonder how many of those who say that to do so amounts to collusion with the Communist tyranny also refuse to buy any smart phone or laptop assembled in China – which would amount to a personal embargo on roughly three quarters of all such devices worldwide.
However to drive a Chinese car is to proclaim your preference for cheapness over principles. Cars in their nature are exercises in public branding, since almost all other road users know which cars are Chinese, which German, and so on. It’s true that the first successful Chinese car here was the all-electric MG, a British brand before it was acquired by Nanjing Automobile in 2005. But the Chinese make no attempt to pretend that those are still British-made cars.
MG-Rover was the last UK-owned volume car manufacturer – we are not like Germany and France, which still have such national champions, and which the EU’s 45 per cent tariffs on Chinese imports are designed to prop up. Readers might recall MG-Rover’s final years in domestic hands: the British government had to deal with a £1bn bankruptcy which left a £500m shortfall in the workers’ pension scheme, while a small group of local West Midlands businessmen (“the Phoenix Four”) had enriched themselves with £42m in pay and bonuses.
Still, I prefer to buy goods from firms which are properly British, if I can – especially if they seem to be based on traditional skills, passed down through the generations. Thus it was that, some months ago, looking for a new kettle, I turned to Morphy Richards. It had a pleasant video on YouTube, with the line “from the kiln to the kitchen”, and highlighted its “ceramic inspiration” against what looked like film of old Staffordshire potteries. From there I went to Amazon, and found what Morphy Richards called a “Clay 1.7litre jug kettle”. I presumed it would be some sort of ceramic kettle. But once delivered and opened, it was revealed as entirely plastic (aside from a wooden base). Flimsy, too.
On further examination (which I should have conducted before purchase), it emerged that in 2023 Morphy Richards, then owned by the Irish company Glen Dimplex, was sold to the Chinese firm Guangdong Xinbao Electrical Appliance Holdings. The corporate finance business handling the transaction hailed “the sale of an iconic British name to a Chinese buyer to secure a prosperous future for the internationally-recognised Morphy Richards brand”.
In fact, the entire manufacturing of Morphy Richards products had been outsourced (as they say) to East Asia 20 years earlier. What changed in 2023 was the ownership of the brand, which means that it is not British in any sense other than its origins.
The Morphy Richards website still opens with a photo of Donal Morphy and Charles Richards, both in black tie outfits, under the headline “When Morphy met Richards”; and the section on “our journey so far” ends: “In 2020 Glen Dimplex Hong Kong opened an office to provide a platform for product sourcing and for further improving the efficiency of operations”. No mention of Chinese ownership.
Interestingly, Morphy Richards remains a member of the body known as BHETA, which stands for British Home Enhancement Trade Association. This must be on the basis that it has an official licensee in the UK, Consumer Brands Ltd, which employs around 30 people to oversee distribution of these Chinese goods here.
Anyway, I immediately returned the non-kiln-related, plastic Chinese kettle back to sender. Yet, when I continued to look at the comments on the product on Amazon UK’s website, there seemed to be many happy purchasers, very few questioning its physical construction, and none observing its 100 per cent Chinese content.
If that’s a guide to public opinion, the Government would be rash to think there would be anything other than outrage from the mass of British voters if it were to impose 45 per cent tariffs on Chinese cars.
What my kettle tells us about Chinese car tariffs
Burnham should heed the lessons of the non-British brand Morphy Richards before penalising the UK’s drivers

articles.summary: China's Rare Earth Leverage Forces EU Into a Sanctions Trade-Off  巴士的報
articles.full_text:
Bloomberg reported on October 14 local time that the EU is negotiating with China. Brussels hopes Beijing will lift sanctions on the small German company Sindlhauser Materials GmbH. That small firm supplies the Dutch ASML, the world's most important chip equipment manufacturer. The sanctions now threaten its survival.
EU seeks China deal to free ASML supplier Sindlhauser.　
The Deal on the Table
      Click to Gallery
        
          
            
            EU seeks China deal to free ASML supplier Sindlhauser.　
          
            
            ASML, Dutch semiconductor equipment giant.
          
            
            Sindlhauser's rare earth supply nearly all Chinese.
          
            
            EU trade chief Šefčovič met Wang Wentao in Beijing.
        
      
    
    
  
  
                        
                            
  
  
    
    Bloomberg cited people in the know as saying the EU will remove trade restrictions on an unnamed Chinese company in exchange. That company is accused of assisting Russia in launching war against Ukraine.
In July this year, China imposed sanctions on Sindlhauser and 13 other European companies. The move retaliated for the EU's 21st round of sanctions against Russia. Sindlhauser is a small German company specializing in precision manufacturing and advanced coating technology for semiconductors and other industries.
In that round of sanctions, the EU listed several Chinese entities as sanctions targets. The EU said they were suspected of providing Russia with key components that could be used to manufacture weapons. Companies placed on the relevant EU and Chinese lists are subject to export controls.
People familiar with the matter said Sindlhauser relies on Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals. If China's sanctions continue, the company will face the risk of bankruptcy within the coming months. It was also said this German company is part of ASML's supply chain.
ASML, Dutch semiconductor equipment giant.
Berlin and Brussels Race to Rescue Sindlhauser
Bloomberg sees a message in China's choice of target. Imposing controls on such an obscure company, the report argues, shows China knows exactly where Europe's economic bottlenecks sit.
An EU official says the European Union has begun discussions with China on whether each side would remove the entities from its own list. That means China's export control framework on one side, and the entities the EU has listed under its own regulations on the other.
The official added that any removal decision on the EU side would require unanimous support from all member states.
The trouble began in July when China's Ministry of Commerce put Sindlhauser on its export control list, and the company's first reaction was panic.
For weeks after the announcement, Sindlhauser had no clear view of whether, or how, it could keep operating.
Help came quickly. According to the people who knows what’s happening, the German government and the Bavarian state government, where Sindlhauser is headquartered, stepped in immediately to help the company find alternative suppliers wherever possible.
The two governments also explored other workarounds, such as recycling existing materials and seeking whatever financial support was available.
Brussels was watching too. Some officials there understood the company's plight and raised the matter with the Chinese side for several weeks.
Sindlhauser's rare earth supply nearly all Chinese.
A Policy Dilemma, an Intelligence Blind Spot
Sindlhauser sits squarely inside China's rare earth grip. According to the report, the company relies almost entirely on Chinese rare earths, and its placement on the export control list dealt a direct blow to its supply chain.
The company had previously taken almost no measures to diversify its supply sources or reduce its dependence on Chinese raw materials.
Some officials see a problem with the rescue. Removing companies such as Sindlhauser from the sanctions list, they worry, could once again weaken the urgency for these European companies to build supply chain networks outside China.
That leaves the German government and EU officials in a bind. Deciding through negotiations which companies go onto or come off trade restriction lists could set a bad precedent for other companies also hoping for sanctions exemptions. It would also mean the EU must make concessions on the question of certain Chinese entities.
But officials involved in handling the matter see a deeper problem. The situation behind the case, they argue, is more concerning, though not surprising.
The explanation: over the past year and a half, China has been collecting information on global supply chains as much as it possibly can. That is how China identified a small company in Bavaria as a supplier to the world's most important chip equipment manufacturer.
Beijing's map of global supply chains runs remarkably deep. The report credits that insight to the licensing system China has built for exports of critical minerals and rare earths.
The system requires foreign companies to submit detailed information, including their customers, how and where Chinese raw materials are used, and photos of the final products.
Germany shows the cost. Some companies have been leaking business secrets to China, while the German government remained completely unaware and unable to obtain the same or even similar information.
More important, the German government still has not formulated any strategy to address its shortcomings in economic intelligence.
A Possible Template, and China's Stated Position
The talks went straight to the top. According to the report, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič visited Beijing last week and met with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The two sides discussed lifting restrictions on Sindlhauser in exchange for relief for a Chinese company.
EU trade chief Šefčovič met Wang Wentao in Beijing.
The backdrop is stark. The EU is hunting for a fix to a massive trade deficit that exceeds $1 billion every single day.
People familiar with the matter say the two sides agreed in Beijing to strengthen information sharing and to give each other advance notice of export restriction measures.
The "one-for-one" arrangement around Sindlhauser, in which each side takes the other's company off its restriction list, could become a template for similar moves in the future. The EU is expected to act first. Only then would China lift its restrictions on the German company.
China's message has stayed consistent. The Chinese side has repeatedly stressed that China holds an objective and impartial position on the Ukraine crisis, stays committed to promoting peace talks, and plays a constructive role in advancing a political resolution of the crisis.
The opposition is just as firm. China firmly rejects the EU's blame-shifting, smears and denigration over the Ukraine crisis. It equally and firmly opposes the EU's unjustified listing and sanctions against Chinese companies and citizens.
Mao Paishou

    Outside 1515 Broadway in Times Square, the usual line mostly leads upstairs to the theater where The Lion King musical has been running for twenty years. But on September 19 local time, this line turned the corner, stretched all the way to the next intersection, and seemed endless.
The Line That Stopped Times Square
The source of the line was not the premiere of a new Broadway show, but a newly opened Chinese camera store.
The store opening that day was the first US flagship store of Chinese imaging brand Insta360. It was also the brand's first directly operated store outside Asia.
Insta360 was founded in Shenzhen in 2015. It first made its name with a camera designed for shooting panoramic footage. Its main products are panoramic and action cameras that do not require cumbersome equipment and can be shared directly after shooting.
In June 2025, it listed on the Shanghai STAR Market. Its market value once exceeded 70 billion yuan, about 76 billion Hong Kong dollars. Industry insiders have called it the world's first listed smart imaging company. Overseas markets contribute about 70 percent of its overall revenue.
The store was originally scheduled to open at noon, but the number of people lining up far exceeded expectations. According to US imaging media outlet PetaPixel, the crowd on the scene that day may have exceeded 1,000 people. The first customer arrived at 2:30 a.m. and waited nearly 10 hours.
One American netizen uploaded footage to social platform X. She described the line as a massive procession that turned two corners. She jogged while high-fiving people in line, and it took her a full 61 seconds to reach the end.
Insta360's New York flagship opening drew massive launch-day crowds.
The young man at the front of the line wants to become a YouTuber. He headed straight to the site after finishing work and queued overnight, becoming the day's 'number one fan.' He received a limited-edition new gimbal camera with an exclusive gold logo.
When asked why he was so enthusiastic about a Chinese brand, his answer captured a recent shift in the US imaging market. He said he used to ride his bike near Central Park a lot. Back then everyone was using GoPro, but now almost everyone has switched to Insta360.
In the line there was also a race car driver who flew nearly 10,000 kilometers from Egypt specifically for this. Egypt still has no Insta360 dealer, and he had tried many places without being able to buy one. So he simply flew directly to New York.

articles.title: No Ukraine aid and EU budget cuts: What does Le Pen mean for the EU? - Euronews
articles.summary: No Ukraine aid and EU budget cuts: What does Le Pen mean for the EU?  Euronews
articles.full_text:
Le Pen is campaigning on a platform that would reshape France’s relationship with the EU ahead of the 2027 presidential election, potentially setting Paris on a collision course with Brussels with far-reaching implications.
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.
On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.
“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.
Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”
He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.
Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.
Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.
Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.
Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.
“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.
“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”
‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’
“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.
He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.
These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.
Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.
“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”
According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.
Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.
Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget
With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.
Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.
Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.
Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.
“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.
Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.
On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.
Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.
Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.
“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.
EU budget for 2028-2034
Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."
She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.
Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.
She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.
Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.
“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.
Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.
“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.
The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.
“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

articles.title: Türkiye seeks inclusion as France, Germany agree on car rules - Hürriyet Daily News
articles.summary: Türkiye seeks inclusion as France, Germany agree on car rules  Hürriyet Daily News
articles.full_text:
Türkiye has been left outside a Franco-German automotive proposal announced on Oct. 16 that would give Britain conditional access to the EU’s planned “Made in EU” support scheme.
The agreement brings France and Germany closer on rules governing which vehicles qualify for public procurement and financial support. For Türkiye, a major production base supplying European markets, the concern extends to future model allocations and factory investment.
The proposal still needs support from other EU member states and the European Parliament before becoming law.
Under the Franco-German plan, the automotive provisions would cover the EU’s 27 members and allow European partners that were part of the single market on Jan. 1, 2020, to opt in.
That definition provides a route for Britain, which left the single market at the end of 2020, but does not include Türkiye.
Participation would require reciprocal treatment and continuing alignment with EU rules on investment from third countries and trade protection.
For Britain, this could mean adopting the bloc’s measures restricting imports of Chinese-made electric and hybrid vehicles.
The agreement narrows a longstanding difference between Paris and Berlin.
France had sought to reserve support for production within the EU, while Germany favored including trading partners closely integrated into European automotive supply chains.
The wider rules are being negotiated under the Industrial Accelerator Act, which would introduce European-content requirements for vehicles benefiting from public purchasing and support schemes.
A joint statement released by French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the aim was to reduce emissions while strengthening Europe’s capacity to develop and manufacture the next generation of electric vehicles.
It linked that transition to investment, research and production in France, Germany and across Europe.
Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa had advocated a similar approach at the Paris Motor Show, calling for incentives for companies investing in European design, research and development, factories and suppliers.
He also urged a swift agreement on emissions rules and measures supporting European production.
The Franco-German compromise combines that industrial preference with concessions on emissions.
It would retain the European Commission’s proposed 90 percent reduction in CO2 emissions from new cars by 2035, compared with 2021 levels, while removing the requirement to offset the remaining emissions through measures such as low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
That change would give manufacturers greater flexibility to continue selling combustion-engine and hybrid vehicles beyond 2035, in line with German industry demands.
For Türkiye, the debate concerns its largest automotive export market. The sector exported $41.5 billion in 2025, with EU countries accounting for $30.1 billion, or 72.5 percent, according to the Uludağ Automotive Industry Exporters’ Association.
Trade Minister Ömer Bolat pressed Türkiye’s case during talks in Brussels earlier in the week.
“Türkiye must be accepted from the very beginning as an equal partner within the framework of the ‘Made with Europe’ concept,” he said on Oct. 14.
Bolat said European companies accounted for nearly 75 percent of Türkiye’s automotive production.
He warned that excluding the country could disrupt the production and supply relationships established through its three-decade customs union with the EU, harming investment, employment and exports on both sides.
The Commission’s March draft already provides for content from customs-union and free-trade partners to receive equivalent treatment in certain procurement and support schemes, subject to conditions.
Bolat said that restrictive automotive provisions nevertheless remained and that Ankara was seeking changes through talks with EU institutions and manufacturers.
Toyota also called for a broader agreement on Oct. 16.
Its European division welcomed discussion of Britain’s inclusion but said the arrangement should extend to other trusted partners, including Türkiye and Japan, whose cooperation could support European competitiveness.
The company said wider inclusion would also benefit future investment decisions, including a battery production study.

Europe’s biggest telecoms companies are teaming up for a new satellite mobile venture to challenge the dominance of Elon Musk’s Starlink.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica and Vodafone are exploring a potential joint venture for the mobile spectrum required to beam mobile phone signals down to Europe from orbiting satellites.
The initiative came amid growing wariness in Europe about relying on Starlink after operator SpaceX last week imposed speed restrictions in Ukraine. The curbs dealt a major setback to the country’s ability to use drones to defend itself from Russian attacks.
The European tie-up would give the companies the combined power to compete against Starlink, which has already begun offering “direct-to-device” services from its constellation of thousands of satellites.
Bosses said the joint venture would help to boost the Continent’s security and resilience in critical communications networks, adding that it would “ensure responsible European governance of key space infrastructure”.
US companies have been leading the development of satellite mobile technology, triggering fears that a handful of US billionaires could end up with control of Europe’s critical infrastructure.

articles.title: Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France - Euronews
articles.summary: Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France  EuronewsCurfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France  BBCFrench riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates  POLITICO.euFrance protests: Curfews issued within several cities after violent riots - as Trump claims he warned Macron  Sky NewsIn pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters  BBC
articles.full_text:
Saturday’s violent protests and looting across France have deepened Macron’s political isolation, raising questions over his authority.
With only months left in his presidency, Emmanuel Macron faces mounting social unrest and political criticism that could ultimately shape his legacy.
After student protests over living conditions erupted into violence last Saturday, Macron has come under fire from across the political spectrum over his handling of the security situation and his response to grievances over education, the cost of living and inflation.
The unrest comes as France grapples with record public debt, soaring fuel prices and escalating international conflicts.
The Yellow Vests movement, which has helped coordinate the protests, announced a “second act” on Monday, with further demonstrations planned for next weekend.
Addressing the nation, Macron condemned violence and announced new operational procedures for security forces.
The Paris prosecutor’s office reported 855 arrests linked to the demonstrations, with 557 people placed in police custody, 433 of whom were adults, representing 78% of those detained.
“Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” Macron said. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”
The response is likely to add to the pressure on Macron, whose performance was viewed unfavourably by 82% of respondents in an Ipsos-BVA poll conducted in October.
The French president is currently on a diplomatic trip to the Gulf, which the Élysée says aims to secure energy supplies as prices rise. However, his decision to leave Paris amid the crisis has drawn criticism, with some accusing Macron of evading the situation.
Le Pen capitalises on chaos
Across the political spectrum, several potential presidential candidates have argued that Macron has lost authority and that his response came too late.
“We have the feeling that the government is collapsing under its own weight, that it is completely overwhelmed,” said Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, which is leading in polls ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election.
Speaking at a press conference at the party’s headquarters on Monday, Bardella pledged tough measures to restore order if the National Rally came to power. “France is caught in a vice between powerlessness and violence,” he said.
Polls put Marine Le Pen ahead of all her potential rivals in the 2027 presidential race. She faced Emmanuel Macron in the 2017 and 2022 run-offs, losing both times.
In the aftermath of the looting, Le Pen said France had been “ravaged” by “an alliance of criminals from the banlieues and politicised professional rioters”.
Le Pen is expected to focus her campaign on migration and law and order, issues that have traditionally resonated with far-right voters, while playing down foreign policy issues such as the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical tensions.
Macron faces criticism from former allies
Macron has also faced criticism from his former prime ministers, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both of whom are running in the 2027 presidential election.
Both are seeking to distance themselves from Macron and his political legacy.
“Like millions of French people, I would have preferred to see decisions and initiatives aimed at restoring order,” Philippe wrote on X.
Attal called on the state to employ all means "so justice is done" including AI facial recognition and deploying the army "if necessary". Macron did not announce extra security measures on Sunday, asking local authorities to coordinate with the police.
The divided French left, riven by internal tensions, accused the government of failing to protect citizens.
“This is unprecedented in its gravity,” Raphaël Glucksmann, a French MEP and social-democratic contender in the 2027 presidential election, told RTL radio. “I had the feeling that France was dissolving, that the Republic was disintegrating, that the state no longer existed.”
Bruno Retailleau, another presidential hopeful representing the conservative Les Républicains party, described Macron as “completely out of his depth, incapable of deploying the full force of the state against the chaos threatening the Republic”.
He cited the arson attack on Limoges town hall and vandalism at Marseille’s town hall.
Senior members of the government have also acknowledged shortcomings in the response.
Police fiasco
On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations. He offered to resign “because I felt responsible for everything that happened”, but Macron rejected his request.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin likewise acknowledged that the authorities had “undoubtedly failed” in their response, citing “shortcomings in intelligence gathering”.
Macron has found few defenders among his former allies, some of whom blame the current political turmoil on his decision to dissolve the National Assembly in June 2024. The move plunged France into political uncertainty, leaving successive governments exposed to the threat of no-confidence votes.
Beyond the immediate security crisis, commentators argue that Macron has alienated young people who helped propel him to power in 2017.
Some protesters have criticised his 2018 high school reforms, arguing that changes to the organisation of specialist subjects have led to longer school days.
In a recent opinion piece, Le Monde described Macron’s relationship with young people as a “major political failure”.
The article drew parallels with the Yellow Vests movement, which erupted in December 2018 amid widespread anger over purchasing power and the rising cost of living.
“Restoring public order is an essential prerequisite for beginning the talks promised on Sunday with all stakeholders and, in doing so, resuming a social dialogue that has been broken for far too long,” the piece concluded.

These are not yet Star Wars, but we may be approaching the first destruction of an enemy satellite in space. Marco Langbroek is a Dutch scientist whose original field was Palaeolithic archaeology. He now works at the prestigious Dutch Delft University of Technology, at its Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, where he observes and tracks objects orbiting the Earth.
