articles.title: Behind US ‘on the run’ anxiety lies Washington’s NATO dilemma - Global Times
articles.summary: Behind US ‘on the run’ anxiety lies Washington’s NATO dilemma  Global Times
articles.full_text:
US NATO Illustration: Liu Rui/GT
Recently, US media outlet The Hill ran a commentary warning that the US is "on the run," citing instances including the redeployment of US bombers stationed in the UK amid security threats, the loss of military aircraft in overseas operations, and Houthi attacks against the King Khalid airport in Saudi Arabia. It also cautions that should Washington relinquish its leadership within NATO, it could be "strategically catastrophic for the alliance."
To characterize US' adjustments as "on the run" may not be entirely accurate. The US still hopes to maintain its global influence, but is increasingly reluctant to foot the bill for it. For Washington, while responsibilities can be shared with Europe, it is unwilling to relinquish its position as alliance leader.
Behind this lie real cost pressures. Long-range strikes and drone threats mean that even bases far from the front lines cannot remain unaffected. While redeploying military aircraft can reduce localized risks, it does not resolve the tension between global commitments and limited resources. With the Middle East continuing to drain military resources and Europe having its own security needs, it is difficult for the US to ensure it can address all fronts simply by increasing its budget. 
Washington is exploring new ways to share this burden. This year's US National Defense Strategy states that NATO allies should assume primary responsibility for conventional defense in Europe, with the US providing critical but more limited support. The so-called NATO 3.0 embodies this adjustment. 
However, while budgetary allocations can be increased, capabilities take years to build up. The pace at which Europe assumes responsibility for conventional defense may not necessarily keep up with the pace at which the US adjusts its deployments. If the US shortens the handover period to lighten its own burden, Europe will also have to shoulder the security risks arising from capability gaps that have not yet been filled. The "burden-sharing" thus carries the implication of shifting risks to allies ahead of time.
Europe's taking on greater responsibility for its own defense could, in principle, offer an opportunity to recalibrate US-EU relations. The crux, however, lies in how power will be distributed once these heavier burdens are assumed.
Questions over where Europe's additional defense spending will be directed, from whom military equipment will be procured, and which security needs will be prioritized all bear directly on European states' own interests. 
If the US is concerned solely with how much its allies spend, yet unwilling to accept greater autonomy for its allies in these decisions, raising defense-spending targets alone will hardly resolve such divergences. Future frictions will increasingly revolve around precisely how these funds should be spent and who gets to make those decisions.
This also points to the deeper problem laid bare by the US "on the run" anxiety. Some US strategists worry that Europe cannot sustain its security without US leadership. Yet Washington uses adjustments to its deployments as a means of exerting pressure, demanding that allies shoulder responsibilities on its terms. The signal that Europe receives is that US security commitments are subject to re-evaluation with every round of bargaining. The deeper the dependence, the greater the unease caused by this uncertainty.
The EU is advancing institutional frameworks centered on joint procurement, defense industrial capacity and defense innovation, while also adopting arrangements to streamline defense regulations and support agile and rapid defense innovation. These measures do not imply that Europe is immediately breaking away from the US, but they do demonstrate that Europe is preparing to expand its own operational capabilities.
The US is therefore forced to face an inescapable dilemma. If Europe's capabilities remain inadequate, it will be difficult for the US to truly offload its burden. However, if Europe's capabilities increase, it will inevitably be in a stronger position to discuss its own priorities. It is difficult to sustain such a relationship in the long term if one demands that Europe possess greater capabilities while expecting it to retain its previous level of deference. 
Washington may adjust its force posture and renegotiate burden-sharing arrangements, yet it cannot offload responsibilities while demanding that allies accept its arrangements unquestioningly. 
What is truly unsustainable is the self-serving desire to retain the old mode of dominance at a lower cost. Much of today's "hegemon's anxiety" in Washington stems from the growing difficulty of realizing that very ambition.
The author is an associate research fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy, Tsinghua University. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

articles.title: France reels from weekend of chaos as violence spreads across Europe - Egypt Independent
articles.summary: France reels from weekend of chaos as violence spreads across Europe  Egypt Independent
articles.full_text:
France is reeling from its worst rioting in years after nationwide protests over education and the cost of living spiraled into a wave of deadly, country-wide violence that has sparked a blame game at home and threatens to spill over into its European neighbors.
Police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into shops and government buildings, with images showing historic buildings ablaze.
More than 2,000 people were arrested, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands. As France begins to count the cost, accusations are mounting that the government failed to adequately anticipate the scale of the crisis, with an election to succeed French President Emmanuel Macron just six months away.
The vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, authorities and political leaders stress – but the level of fighting and destruction, the worst seen in years, has shaken the nation and prompted forceful condemnations from leaders and the public alike.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said on Sunday evening. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
He also promised to hold meetings this week to discuss “concrete proposals” and to listen to protesters’ demands. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to stem the protests in France – as well as similar demonstrations against costs of living now spreading in other countries nearby.
How did this begin?
It all began in September with a strike by students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs, who demanded more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
Students around the country, long frustrated with an understaffed and overcrowded education system, launched protests that at times turned violent. A heavy-handed police response fueled public anger and pushed hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, especially after videos of a police officer using a banned headlock on a girl.
Within a few weeks, the protests swelled to become a broader movement beyond students, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
“This can’t go on,” said 57-year-old Maria Pallas, a member of a major French trade union, speaking to CNN at Saturday’s protest in Paris. “There’s the cost of living. There’s unemployment. There’s a bunch of things. A young person will go looking for work, we’ll promise him a lot, and he’ll end up with nothing.”
Over half a million people hit the streets across France on Saturday. For the most part, things were peaceful; far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the crowd in Paris as “moving calmly.”
But in several locations the protests spilled into violence, especially as night fell. In Paris, groups of masked young people looted shops and started fires; in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office; in the central city of Limoges, the spire of a 143-year-old town hall collapsed in flames, reviving painful memories for some of the Notre Dame Cathedral fire.
The protests subsided somewhat on Sunday, with small pockets flaring, and police firing tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, one of the largest public squares in Paris.
By the end of the weekend, Paris looked like a “war zone,” one visitor to the city told Reuters. Residents across the capital were stunned, with some condemning the looters and rioters, and others placing blame with authorities who failed to address the crisis earlier.
“It’s heartbreaking, heartbreaking seeing our city like this,” said 59-year-old Marseille resident Farida, who did not give a last name, according to Reuters. “If every protest ends with all the shop windows smashed and stores trashed, this simply cannot go on — it cannot go on.”
One Paris resident, 56-year-old Paola Formenti, voiced support for the protesters’ “legitimate” anger. The violence “has to be condemned, of course,” she said – but added, “I think the only way of actually avoiding this kind of violence is to answer to the protests of the people, to listen to them.”
In his Sunday address, Macron acknowledged protesters’ grievances and said he would take “a number of international initiatives” to tackle fuel prices and ensure a stable supply from Gulf nations. He did not make any concrete assurances or give further specifics.
What comes next and will it spread?
The protests and fallout could shape France’s upcoming election next spring. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed this weekend that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Mélenchon, has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
Protesters have taken to the streets elsewhere in Europe this weekend, too.
In Belgium, students demonstrated against the state of their education system. In Lisbon, Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched on Saturday to protest rising costs of living and the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, Milan also saw two consecutive nights of unrest this weekend with protesters throwing stones and looting supermarkets, and police responding with tear gas and water cannons.
Meanwhile in Albania, students have been taking to the streets for months, protesting perceived government corruption. Demonstrations in the capital Tirana turned violent this weekend, with one person photographed throwing a Molotov cocktail at riot police.
Authorities in many of these countries have condemned the violence and called for calm. The protests have caught the attention of the White House, with Vice President JD Vance posting a video of the burning Limoges town hall on X and blaming the unrest on failed immigration policy.
US President Donald Trump also mentioned the protests during a rally in Georgia this weekend, joking: “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5,000 there,” referring to the dividend promised if the Republicans win the midterm elections.
CNN’s Joseph Ataman, Catherine Nicholls, Sana Noor Haq, James Legge, and Melissa Bell contributed to this report.

The rules apply to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026. Pulp and paper are within scope, so most packaging producers selling into Europe will need a reliable way to prove where their materials come from.
Monro will use Finboot's MARCO Track & Trace platform to collect data from suppliers, assess deforestation risk and submit the required Due Diligence Statements to the EU's TRACES system, all in one place. Monro has supplied FSC®-certified, responsibly sourced packaging to well-known retail and cosmetics brands since 1985 and will use MARCO to manage its EUDR compliance and give customers confidence in the products they buy.
For paper and packaging producers, MARCO will:
• Gather verified, geolocated data from suppliers.
• Assess and monitor deforestation risk across the supply chain.
• File Due Diligence Statements to the EU TRACES system.
• Keep a full audit trail for regulators and customers.
Matt Sibson, Chief Commercial Officer of Monro, said: “Our customers rely on us to source responsibly on their behalf. EUDR sets a higher bar, and MARCO lets us show exactly where our materials come from.”
Juan Miguel Pérez, CEO and co-founder of Finboot, said: “Paper and packaging is one of the sectors most affected by EUDR. Monro has taken the sensible route of putting the right systems in place early, so that compliance becomes part of how the business runs rather than a last-minute scramble.”
Nish Kotecha, Chair of Finboot, said: “EUDR affects almost every company that works with paper and packaging. Getting traceability right does more than tick a box. It gives you a supply chain you can stand behind, and the evidence to prove it to regulators, customers and investors.”
Paper, packaging and pulp companies preparing for EUDR can request a demo and try MARCO on their own supply chain at www.finboot.com/eudr. Find out more about Monro and its approach to responsible sourcing by following this link: www.monro.co.uk.

articles.title: UK Pays Record Sums to Balance Grid as Transmission Falls Behind - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: UK Pays Record Sums to Balance Grid as Transmission Falls Behind  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comBritain must ‘rely on EU to keep lights on’ this winter  The TelegraphCost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day | Energy industry  The GuardianQuestions over power supply as Neso faces ‘unprecedented’ turmoil  The TimesThe UK Is Paying More Than Ever to Steady a Straining Power Grid  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
The UK is among the most ambitious states when it comes to a transition to a net-zero economy. Also, the UK is struggling with some of the highest electricity prices in Europe—and is paying significant sums to maintain grid balance, even when its wind installations are generating plenty of electricity.
Normally, the cost of maintaining a balanced grid, meaning stable and secure supply of electricity, is the highest when the weather affects alternative energy sources. In winter, for instance, solar panels do not generate as much as they do during the summer, and with insufficient baseload backup, the UK needs to boost imports and pay the price. Also, winter is the so-called dark doldrums season for wind, meaning less wind and lower wind speeds. This also increases demand for imported electricity for the UK, leading to a fatter electricity bill.
However, it seems that fatter electricity bills for the UK could come even with abundant domestic electricity generation—because the electricity generated cannot get to where it is needed. Bloomberg called it “bottlenecks” in a recent article detailing an occurrence that highlighted one of the inherent drawbacks of alternative energy, namely, the fact that wind and solar capacity needs to be built where there are suitable weather patterns and not near demand centers, which is where baseload capacity gets built, shortening the distance between demand and supply points. Related: China’s Solar Exports Keep Falling as Beijing Mulls Export Controls
However, a baseload power plant, whether coal, gas, or nuclear, can be built almost anywhere, as long as there is a river nearby. In this respect, baseload generation capacity is a lot more flexible. With wind and solar, the installations need to be put up in locations that get a lot of wind and, respectively, solar. Given the conversion factors of both, especially solar, compromise on the location would automatically turn into compromise on the amount of generation. In other words, wind and solar are much more geographically bound than baseload power plants.
In the UK’s case, most wind turbines are located in the north, in Scotland. Yet the biggest demand centers, including London, are far to the south and southeast. Getting the electricity generated in Scotland to London is a challenge because, as Bloomberg put it, the UK “is adding wind farms faster than it can construct the infrastructure needed to carry that power south.” In other words, companies are building turbines, but they are not building transmission lines—and if they were, this would have led to higher electricity bills again.
This time, the higher bills come from the need for urgent imports—while the UK was exporting electricity generated in the south to France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, Bloomberg noted in its report. Those urgent imports on that day resulted in additional costs equivalent to $51.2 million for balancing the UK grid—on just one day. Last month, the total grid balance bill for the country hit an all-time high of some 500 million pounds, or $666 million. This month, that record could get broken, according to energy transition consultancy LCP Data, which supplied the figures to Bloomberg. There is no quick fix for this problem.
“These wind farms were built with very limited consideration of where that electricity would be consumed,” according to Jason Mann, managing director at business consultancy FTI Consulting. “Those costs are locked in for generations.” True as this might be, it bears repeating that building wind turbines close to demand centers where there is not a lot of wind would be rather unproductive.
This puts the UK and other transitioning countries in quite a bind. On the one hand, they have prioritized the decarbonization of their grid and industries. On the other, they need the grid stable and the industries functioning—which cannot happen with unstable and expensive electricity supply. Pursuing both requires a lot of money, and it will be consumers who pay it.
Earlier this month, the UK’s energy regulator Ofgem activated a mechanism aimed at shielding electricity suppliers from excessive volatility on the wholesale market. The mechanism involves “compensating suppliers that bought energy in advance if customers switch to cheaper deals,” according to a Reuters report. Essentially, Ofgem will be paying companies that bought expensive electricity before a sharp drop on the wholesale market, exposing them to an outflow of customers seeking lower bills from other suppliers.
In other words, the UK’s grid has become exceedingly complicated at a time of geopolitical upheaval that is making all energy more expensive because, whether the UK government likes it or not, hydrocarbons still underpin all energy prices. There is no easy or cheap solution to the problem. The only viable one is expanding the grid itself, by building more transmission lines from electricity production hubs to demand hubs—and finding a way not to saddle consumers with the billions this will cost.
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

Putin suggested the meeting during a phone call with Mr Trump on Oct 9, when the US president agreed to buy Russian diesel and waive sanctions on Moscow, according to a Russian intelligence officer who spoke to The Wall Street Journal.

Government borrowing cost have risen across Europe after riots in France sent ripples through financial markets.
The yield on 10-year French government bonds rose from 4.80pc to 4.93pc on Monday after violent protests over the cost of living and poor conditions in schools led to more than 2,000 arrests over the weekend.
France saw the sharpest increase in bond yields – the effective interest rate paid to borrow – among G7 nations but unease spread well beyond its borders.
In Italy, the cost for Rome to borrow over 10 years rose from 4.49pc to 4.57pc after protesters clashed with police in Milan over the weekend.
Spain’s 10-year yield rose from 4.03pc to 4.07pc ahead of a general strike over housing and wages planned for Nov 11, less than three weeks before a snap general election on Nov 29.
Even Britain’s 10-year gilt yield rose from 5.37pc to 5.43pc, despite the comparatively lower threat of unrest.
Andrew Kenningham, the chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, said France was heading towards a fiscal crisis that risked tipping the eurozone into recession.

articles.title: How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?  Al JazeeraWhy are people protesting across Europe?  The GuardianViolent protests multiply across Europe  Financial TimesWhat is behind the breakdown in Western society  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting CorporationAll the European cities on fire after a weekend of violent protests  The Independent
articles.full_text:
Student protests in France are into their second month, escalating into demonstrations across Europe.
What began in September in France with pupils protesting against overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages has grown into wider anger at the cost of living and planned cuts to public services.
Protesters in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain have also taken to the streets over the lack of affordable housing, rising costs and failing public services – with many young people saying they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.
Facing their anger are leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez and Portugal’s PM Luis Montenegro. Sanchez belongs to the left, Meloni to the right and Macron and Montenegro are conservative-leaning centrists. But while their politics vary, they all face mounting unrest because of soaring costs of living.
Are they out of touch with the experiences and sentiments of youth in their countries? Al Jazeera visualises how prices, wages, housing and education have changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over the past 26 years, from when Macron, Meloni, Sanchez and Montenegro were in their 20s, much like many of the protesters angry with them.
How much more expensive is it compared to 2000?
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
Spain recorded the steepest increase at 78 percent, followed by Portugal at 71 percent, 68 percent in Italy and France at 59 percent.
That means goods and services that cost 100 euros ($112) in 2000 now cost about 178 euros ($200) in Spain, 171 euros ($192) in Portugal, 168 euros ($188) in Italy and 159 euros ($178) in France.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy, 8.3 percent in Spain, 8.1 percent in Portugal and 5.9 percent in France, the highest rate in all four countries since at least 2000.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By October that year, eight months into the war, energy prices across the eurozone were almost 42 percent higher than a year earlier, and food prices were also rising sharply, according to Eurostat.
Between 2021 and 2023, prices increased by 12 to 15 per cent in the four countries. Wages failed to keep up, and because prices do not fall back once inflation eases, many households are still feeling the squeeze today.
How have salaries changed?
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 per cent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 per cent in Spain, 11 per cent in France and 20 per cent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.
In Spain most new jobs were in tourism and services, and were often seasonal and poorly paid, Jaime Velazquez, a journalist in Madrid, told Al Jazeera’s Inside Story.
Julius Fintelmann, cofounder and editor-in-chief of The European Correspondent, said ageing societies were squeezing out opportunities for younger workers, adding that the pay gap between older and younger workers has been widening across high-income economies for decades, so the promise that each generation would be better off than the last no longer holds.
How has the cost of housing changed?
Housing has become harder to afford in all four countries since 2000, according to the OECD’s price-to-income ratio. It provides a broad picture of how house prices have changed relative to incomes over time. When prices rise faster than incomes, the ratio goes up, suggesting homes are becoming less affordable on average.
However, it doesn’t show which households or regions are hit hardest, does not account for mortgage and borrowing costs, and says nothing about the quality of the homes people are paying for.
Spain has seen the biggest change. Its price-to-income ratio is 56 per cent higher than in 2000, even after falling sharply following the 2008 financial crisis.
In France, the ratio is 39 per cent higher than in 2000, though it has eased slightly since peaking in 2022.
Italy is the exception where house prices have broadly kept pace with incomes, leaving the ratio just 5 per cent higher than in 2000.
Portugal has seen the sharpest change in recent years. Its price-to-income ratio fell steadily for 15 years after 2000, meaning homes became more affordable. But since 2015 the ratio has risen by 67 per cent.
The OECD publishes the price-to-income ratio with 2015 as its reference year. To compare it with the wage and price data in this article, which started in 2000, Al Jazeera has reset the figures so that 2000 = 100.
How has state expenditure on education changed?
Education has been at the heart of the unrest in France, where protests began because of overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. While in Belgium and Albania, demonstrators have rallied against the rising cost of education and access to universities.
According to the latest data from Eurostat, France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.6 per cent in 2000.
Italy spent 4.4 per cent of its GDP on education compared to 4 per cent in 2024, Spain spent 4.1 per cent in 2000 and the same in 2024. Portugal spent 4.8 per cent in 2000 and 4.3 per cent in 2024.

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
Ukraine received intelligence from western partners about just one of two Russian ballistic missile attacks overnight into Monday, as relations between Kyiv and Washington have sharply deteriorated in recent days.
More than 200 drones and several “Banderol” cruise missiles targeted energy facilities in 11 regions, leading to power outages for about 550,000 households, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a report by Ukraine’s air force.
Kyiv residents heard explosions in two distinct waves on Sunday night. Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said there had been no warning about the first wave of ballistic missiles, but said the country’s air defence and authorities had received warnings about the second one.
Ukraine’s air force said it had only managed to shoot down four missiles overnight.
Russia’s defence ministry said it had fired drones and ground-launched missiles at what it claimed were defence infrastructure sites in Kyiv, as well as a data centre. The ministry said it also struck a ship approaching the port of Odesa that it claimed was carrying military and dual-use cargo.
A 21-year-old woman died in the attack on Kyiv, according to Ukraine’s emergency services. The Datagroup company confirmed that one of its data centres had been destroyed in Kyiv overnight. A metro station on the city’s left bank was also damaged in the attack.
Zelenskyy’s dispute with Donald Trump over the US president’s decision to relax economic sanctions on Russia deepened on Monday.
“When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine’s air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” Zelenskyy said.
The statement came hours after Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that the Ukrainian president did not want “to end this war”.
Zelenskyy had said on Sunday that intelligence sharing from the US had resumed after a brief pause. Ukraine is particularly reliant on US satellites to detect the launch of ballistic missiles able to reach major Ukrainian cities in mere minutes.
Kyiv has also accused Washington of introducing speed limits to the Starlink communication systems. The satellite-based system operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX is ubiquitous in Ukraine’s armed forces, and allows Ukrainian forces to fly drones targeting Russian positions and vehicles as well as drones.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio denied on Sunday that Washington had introduced restrictions.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Starlink devices were still failing “in various sectors of the front” when a drone reached a speed of 130kph.
“This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered Shaheds,” Zelenskyy wrote on X in reference to the Russian drone based on the Iranian Shahed model.

This article from the Daily Caller News Foundation
By Jillian Butler
A hard-fought trade deal between Europe and Beijing is emerging, but it’s unclear if the agreement will change what has become a stark economic reality for the continent.
European Union (EU) envoys agreed to a broad, tentative deal with Beijing in October, which would cut Chinese hybrid car exports in half, Reuters reports. But the potential deal comes off as a pyrrhic victory for Europe, as much of the continent’s industry remains intimately tied to China, including the automotive industry and critical mineral mining.
“While this is being ballyhooed by the EU as a great deal, the fact is that 350,000 Chinese hybrids coming into the EU market is still a lot of cars,” energy consultant David Blackmon told the DCNF, “no doubt the European carmakers will grasp at any relief but the deal really isn’t any magic bullet protecting them from Chinese intrusion into what used to be their market.”
While China controls the supply chain for batteries and critical minerals, Europe struggles to maintain a similar level of production.
“We are more than 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials [and] 90% for some rare earths,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at a September State of the Union Address, according to POLITICO.
“It’s making life a bit more difficult for the Chinese, but … that’s not going to stop them as it happened to the electric cars,” Felipe Munoz of Car Industry Analysis told Reuters.
Europe has grown dependent on Chinese automotive exports, specifically with hybrid vehicles. China’s exports of hybrids to the 27 EU member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of 2026–triple the $2.5 billion in 2025.
That is almost nine times higher than the $845 million exported in 2021, according to Reuters.
“The number one goal of the Chinese Communist Party is accumulating power. Dependence has to run in one direction only – toward Beijing. Deindustrializing other countries is a means to this end because it renders these countries reliant on China. The Chinese Communist Party accomplishes this through a range of means, including by co-opting elites and competing unfairly — e.g., the Party supports (including through espionage) and subsidizes national-champion firms to enable them to underprice competitors abroad,” Jacqueline Neal, President of the Long Term Strategy Group told the DCNF, “these firms can then capture markets and through that, render other countries dependent on Chinese products, delivering leverage to the Party.”
The European Union did not respond to a request for comment.
The consequences of Chinese dependence are perhaps no more apparent than in Germany.
Once a hub for the automotive industry, the country now struggles to cope with American tariffs and compete with China — a country that was once a lucrative export market. In the mid 2010s, the number of automobiles manufactured in Germany began to dwindle, as German manufacturers began to build factories in Hungary, China, and Mexico. By the first half of 2026, BMW reported a 20% decline and Mercedes a 28% decline, according to New York Times.
Previously, China was a profitable customer for Germany, with it accounting for 37% of all Volkswagen sales in 2019. In 2025, that figure dwindled to 30%. Interest in western cars has declined among the Chinese as companies such as BYD and Geely Auto developed cars quicker and cheaper while being promoted by the Chinese government.
“Despite better products, we cannot match the cost and pricing of export models from China”, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume told his employees in July, according to the New York Times.
China’s also bought significant stakes in German auto companies, with Chinese state owned automotive manufacturer, BAIC, owning a roughly 10% stake in Mercedes, Automotive World reports.
“Europe is going to a point where they will need to decide whether they’re doing what the US is doing or just let the whole industry be bought by the Chinese,” Munoz explained to Reuters, referring to America’s restrictions on Chinese-made automobiles, including a 100% tariff on electric vehicles.
The deal does not appear to deter Beijing.
Zhao Fei, president of Chinese automotive company Changan, said that he was “not that concerned,” and could set up production in Europe to circumvent the export cap.
“This actually provides opportunities for Chinese companies like Changan to enter the European market,” Fei told Reuters, adding that the company is planning to manufacture its first cars in the region in early 2027.
The EU-China deal also includes China dropping its tariff on auto parts, and would continue to fast-track licenses to export rare-earth elements to the EU, POLITICO reports.

articles.summary: UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards  The GuardianStronger safeguards for wheelchair users and better-trained staff to support disabled air passengers  GOV.UKDfT Sets Out Planned Aviation Accessibility Reforms Alongside AAIG Report  DM NewsICAO calls for more accessible air travel worldwide  Regional GatewayBritain plans to scrap compensation cap for damaged wheelchairs — The Guardian  UA.NEWS

Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff.
A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson demanded action to improve air travel in response to numerous incidents in which passengers had been left stranded without assistance.
The Department for Transport said airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month.
Almost one in five disabled passengers are still dissatisfied with their air travel experience though, according to an industry body, and requests for assistance are continuing to rise.
The government is planning to remove the maximum payout in compensation for lost and damaged wheelchairs, and to give the aviation regulator new powers to fine airlines and airports when passengers are not given the assistance they need to travel.
The changes are expected to be in the civil aviation bill which is progressing through parliament and which the government said would give air passengers stronger protection and consumer rights.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “People must be able to fly with dignity and peace of mind. For disabled passengers this means not worrying about their wheelchair coming back in one piece, or whether staff will be there to support them around the airport.
“We’ve backed industry to overhaul staff training, prevent damage to mobility aids and create easy, simple ways for passengers to share key information before they fly.”
The co-chairs of the aviation accessibility implementation group, which is assessing progress on the 19 recommendations in Grey-Thompson’s report, said: “There is much more to be done, but we have made a positive start. We will be focusing now on embedding more of the changes that are needed to enable disabled people to fly with confidence and dignity.”
The chief executive of lobby group Airlines UK, Tim Alderslade, said the number of passengers requiring assistance was up nearly 10% year on year.
“82% report that they are satisfied with their air travel experience which demonstrates the efforts and progress airlines are making for those who require additional support when they fly,” he said.

articles.summary: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports  The GuardianChina economy: Growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness  BBCWorld in Brief: France’s cabinet gathers over protests; China’s healthy GDP growth  The EconomistChina's economic growth picks up as exports boom, consumers balk  ReutersChina’s economy picks up pace with 4.5% growth  Financial Times

Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.
Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.

The agreement's tariff provisions are expected to be phased in according to specific schedules. Norway's government said approximately half of its exports to Vietnam would qualify for duty-free treatment when the agreement takes effect, with that proportion exceeding 98% within seven years.
Those figures apply specifically to Norwegian exports to Vietnam, rather than all goods traded between Vietnam and the four EFTA members. articles.title: How the Climate Crisis Fueled the Youth Protests Roiling France - The Energy Mix
articles.summary: How the Climate Crisis Fueled the Youth Protests Roiling France  The Energy Mix
articles.full_text:
By the time Cléo made it to Greek class, she had gone completely pale. It was a Wednesday in June during France’s second consecutive heat wave this year, and the 16-year-old was struggling to cope with the rising temperatures.
She pushed through, thinking she was just tired. But the following day at her sweltering high school on the eastern edge of Paris, nausea and a desperate thirst gripped her. The school nurse, recognizing the signs of heat exhaustion, told her to go home.
This week, as she recalled the experience and worried about more heat waves to come, Cléo and her friends stood by a pile of green garbage cans, blocking their school’s entrance. For the past four weeks, scenes like this have multiplied at thousands of schools across France, where students are protesting to demand better learning conditions and more investment in public education.
These student protests have become one of the most significant social movements in the country’s recent history. They’ve been met with a heavy-handed police crackdown; Roughly 8,000 arrests have been made in three weeks, 85% of them minors. Fearing repercussions, Cléo and other underage students who talked to Inside Climate News asked to be quoted using only their first names.
The students’ demands are far-ranging: more teachers, smaller class sizes, a shortened school day and an overhaul of the post-secondary college application system. But the heart of the revolt is indignation over crumbling school infrastructure—a problem laid bare by climate-change-fueled heat waves.
This year was France’s hottest on record, and the country counted 8,000 excess deaths during the summer’s heat waves. In June alone, deaths spiked 11% compared to the same month in 2025.
France’s schools, meanwhile, were not built for the hotter world the students have inherited after generations of fossil fuel use have warped the climate. Many buildings were designed to hold onto heat; air conditioning is rare. As classrooms recorded temperature peaks above 100 degrees Fahrenheit this spring, schools reported incidents from fainting to nosebleeds.
Students protesting this week outside high schools in the Paris area described a raft of problems in their buildings that made them feel abandoned by their government, including falling ceilings, moldy walls, out-of-service bathrooms, chair shortages and pest infestations. For many, this year’s record heat waves were a breaking point that highlighted their schools’ inability to keep students safe in a warming climate.
“We’re here to claim our rights, we’re here to make ourselves heard because we’re fed up with this government, we’re fed up with this country and we’ve had enough,” said Koumba, a 16-year-old student at a high school in Montreuil, on the outskirts of Paris.
Schools Built for an Outdated Climate
Marie-Hélène Azam is a professor of engineering science at the National Institute of Applied Sciences and leads a project studying how France’s primary school buildings can be adapted to withstand heat waves.
“We’re realizing that, until now, we’ve designed buildings for energy efficiency in winter,” she said. “We need to find a way to reconcile comfort in winter with comfort in summer, and that means designing buildings a little differently.”
Traditionally, French schools have large windows to maximize sunlight and warmth. That backfires when temperatures rise, turning classrooms into greenhouses.
And like many older buildings in France, schools are typically heavy structures with “high thermal inertia,” absorbing, storing and then releasing heat. This is beneficial during winter, but it can make classrooms hotter inside than out on high-heat days.
The issue isn’t just extreme temperatures. The way they’re hitting makes it worse.
“With heat waves becoming more intense and lasting longer, we no longer have enough time to cool these buildings down at night or between two heat waves,” Azam said. “As soon as the temperature of the building starts to drop, another even more intense heat wave arrives.”
Among potential solutions: exterior shutters to prevent the sun from heating up windows, ceiling fans to cool students and evaporative cooling technologies that use water to zap heat.
A spokesperson for the Île-de-France region, which oversees public high school infrastructure in the Paris area, said it allocated $1.2 billion to school construction and renovations this year, including upgrades to roofs and windows. During the heat waves, the regional government spent $1.1 million to open additional exam centers and purchase misting devices and fans.
In France, air conditioning has so far been treated as a last resort for climate adaptation. Many worry that widespread installation will worsen the “urban heat island” effect that makes cities hotter than rural areas: AC units push hot air outside, increasing temperatures on the streets. Cost is another barrier, with energy prices in Europe among the highest in the world.
Climate Anxiety Beyond the Classroom
The protesting students aren’t focused on air conditioning. Instead, many say they know the heat doesn’t start and end in the classroom, and it will follow them long after they graduate.
Many of them cite climate change as a source of anxiety about their future, alongside concerns about the economy and how artificial intelligence will affect their job prospects.
On Tuesday, Margaux Levy and Raphaëlle Richard marched alongside hundreds of thousands of protesters across France. The two are among the many university students joining high schoolers, hoping leaders will listen to the younger generation’s concerns.
They sat on a patch of grass, holding signs, as other protesters flooded the Place Vauban in Paris’ 7th borough.
Heat waves “are unpleasant,” said Levy, a second-year university student. “That said, I think the problem can be addressed primarily through environmental measures. I don’t think installing air conditioning in high schools is a good long-term solution, because it only makes the problem worse.”
She added, “It’s pretty unsettling to see that we’re living in a world where we’re going to die out because of our own actions. We’re making no effort, and I’m not trying to be pessimistic about this, but everything seems pretty bleak. I feel like nobody is going to make an effort, and political parties aren’t making it a priority.”
Raised on warnings about climate change, the protesters are watching the crisis as it unfolds.
“We’ve talked about [climate change] a lot, but we weren’t really seeing the consequences firsthand yet. Now, after the major heat waves we’ve experienced, we’re seeing the deaths it causes,” said Richard, a second-year student in medical school. “The awareness is growing, but it needs to be accompanied by necessary political measures.”
Earlier that day, Swedish environmental and social activist Greta Thunberg joined students protesting in Paris, visiting a school on the northern edge of the city.
“This generation is one that has been growing up with a sense of hopelessness,” she told The Associated Press. “We can see our future and our rights taken from us in front of our very eyes. What do they expect? Of course people are going to fight back.”

U.S. defense firm Anduril could eventually manufacture its newly unveiled Steelfin interceptor missiles in Europe, a company executive said this week, as governments aim to expand air defense production after global conflicts highlighted shortages of interceptor missiles.
“I certainly hope that something like Steelfin could become a capability that we engage with both the Polish customer and industry,” Brian Moran, Anduril’s vice president for Europe, told Reuters on Monday.
“We would definitely consider engaging European partners and customers on this capability.” Steelfin is due to undergo flight testing in 2027, according to Anduril.
Wars in Ukraine and the Gulf have strained stocks of air defense interceptor missiles and caused delivery delays.
Moran said Anduril saw Steelfin as a complementary system that could provide a more affordable interceptor alongside existing missile defense systems like the Patriot and others.
The company is already in talks to establish production in Poland of its Barracuda-500 cruise missile, and Moran said that experience could open the door to additional manufacturing projects.
“We’re having a very good experience with our industry partner here, PGZ,” he said, adding that discussions were also under way with the defense ministry and other government agencies. PGZ is Poland’s state-owned arms group.
Poland, one of NATO’s top defense spenders relative to the size of its economy, is seeking to expand domestic arms production and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.
Moran said talks with PGZ, its WZL-2 unit and the government were focused on balancing local production with delivery speed and Poland’s specific military requirements.
Asked about growing calls in Europe for defense industrial sovereignty, Moran said the term could mean different things, from security of supply and maintenance capabilities to control over software upgrades and future modifications.
“Sovereignty has a cost. There’s a cost to localization. There’s cost in terms of timing and just schedule. And those need to be considered in light of the threats that Europe collectively is facing.”
While governments also want economic benefits from defense spending, the military outcome is most important, he said, adding that greater localization can come with additional costs and longer timelines.

articles.title: Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee - Disruption Banking
articles.summary: Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee  Disruption Banking
articles.full_text:
IMF Annual Meetings, 17 October 2026
Introduction
The global economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of high uncertainty. The conflict in the Middle East continues to expose energy markets to sharp swings. Trade tensions and protectionist measures are weighing on confidence and contributing to a reconfiguration of trade flows. The global economy has held up thanks in part to the rise of artificial intelligence, with investment in technology supporting activity and trade, particularly in economies integrated into technology value chains. Risks nonetheless remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation. A return to an international economic order grounded in openness, predictability and the rule of law would help trade and investment flourish.
Economic activity
Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. Growth was broad-based across most euro area countries and sectors in the first half of 2026. The September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.
As the energy shock fades over the medium term, the projections see domestic demand benefitting from a recovery in real income over the medium term, driven by lower energy inflation and a resilient labour market. Rising government spending on infrastructure and defence, complemented by investment in AI and digital technologies, should also support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand, also driven by AI.
The medium-term outlook is surrounded by uncertainty over how intense and long-lasting the Middle East conflict will be, and how the resulting shocks might propagate through the economy. Risks to growth are assessed to be on the downside.
Fiscal sustainability remains a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. It is important to maintain sound fiscal policies, including by adhering to fiscal rules, and, where debt is high, to consolidate, re-prioritise spending and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of public finances to rebuild buffers. Governments should strive to ensure that any fiscal response to the energy shock is temporary, targeted and tailored.
In addition, policies that strengthen resilience to climate change can improve the economy’s ability to absorb climate-related shocks. These efforts should be complemented by structural policies that promote labour market participation, equip the workforce with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy and facilitate the diffusion of new technologies. Priorities include advancing the savings and investments union, improving access to risk capital and creating better conditions for innovative firms to scale up across the Single Market.
Inflation
Headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, mostly reflecting a surge in energy inflation, and, to a lesser extent, an increase in food and services inflation. Core inflation increased slightly to 2.5%. The range of underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September and wages have so far shown no material response to the energy shock.
Looking ahead, higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027 and to gradually feed through to core and food inflation. Headline inflation is expected to decline after the first quarter as energy inflation falls, returning to around target towards the end of 2027. The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. A more intense or persistent energy shock could strengthen indirect and second-round effects, resulting in higher and more persistent inflation. Extreme weather could push up food prices. By contrast, a sustainable resolution of geopolitical conflicts, weaker energy pass-through or more risk-averse financial markets could lower inflation.
Monetary policy
The Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, following an increase of the same size in June.
Our interest rate decisions are based on our reaction function, which comprises three criteria: our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, the dynamics of underlying inflation; and the strength of monetary policy transmission.
The inflation outlook points to higher inflation ahead, especially in the short term, given the latest developments in energy markets. However, we see no evidence at this stage of significant pass-through of energy prices to other prices and wages, beyond what we have already included in our projections. And while growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting. This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise.
Taking these three criteria together, the energy shock is too large to “look through” but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check.
In setting future policy, we will make a comprehensive assessment of the incoming data based on our reaction function. In July, the Governing Council decided on the operational features and the onboarding process for the enhanced EUREP, the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks that was announced earlier this year. The new facility supports the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforces the international role of the euro. More than 30 central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months.
Financial stability
Sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high. Continued geopolitical tensions, fiscal challenges and uncertainties around accelerated AI adoption continue to be causes for concern. The widespread concentration of critical third-party service providers introduces single points of failure for both financial and non-financial institutions. New frontier AI models have increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities.
Euro area banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers and robust profitability, together with healthy and stable asset quality. These solid fundamentals should help navigate ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and effectively support lending to the economy. Strengthened prudential regulation and supervision since the global financial crisis has helped leave euro area banks in a strong position to withstand the unfolding economic challenges.
Shocks could expose vulnerabilities among non-bank financial intermediaries, notably from concentrated AI-related exposures, amplifying market stress and creating spillovers across financial sectors. Banks’ exposures to non-banks and vulnerable firms could expose funding and credit vulnerabilities.
Stress in private credit markets has continued, with private credit funds reporting outflows and reactivating redemption gates. Private market “semi-liquid funds” that allow for redemptions are becoming more prevalent, which could lead to greater liquidity mismatches in the future, but euro area financial institutions have limited direct exposure to private credit. This means, for now, that private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area.
Payment systems
Central bank money must evolve to fulfil the needs of an increasingly digital economy. The Eurosystem is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing the stability and trust of central bank money to digital retail payments and tokenised finance in Europe. In the retail space we are preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent – the digital euro – for day-to-day payments. The digital euro will further stimulate innovation and competition in retail payments, ensuring that the continued co-existence of public and private solutions underpins Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments. To lay the groundwork for a seamless and secure launch, we will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key to making this possible.
In the wholesale space, the Eurosystem is developing new capabilities to ensure that central bank money can settle transactions in the growing market of tokenised assets. Pontes – the Eurosystem’s distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution that went live on 21 September – marks the first step in implementing our strategy to enable the development of a European tokenised ecosystem. This vision will be advanced under the Appia initiative, which aims to deliver a blueprint for this ecosystem based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance.
International cooperation
We value the work of our global institutions and fora, particularly those that promote global macroeconomic and financial stability. We welcome the recent completion of the three major IMF reviews (Comprehensive Surveillance Review, Financial Sector Assessment Program Review and Review of Program Design and Conditionality), which strengthen the role of the IMF at the centre of the global financial safety net. Climate-related work should remain fully anchored in IMF operations, particularly surveillance. Multilateral efforts to help tackle global imbalances support coordination of domestic action that is required to minimise the risks from disorderly adjustment. The IMF’s analytical work on global imbalances and its improvements to the methodology for assessing external balances provide a strong basis for these efforts.

After a lengthy hiatus, negotiations resumed last year amid global uncertainty over US tariffs and culminated in an agreement in July.
This trade deal marks a significant step forward in Vietnam’s diplomatic and economic relations with the four European countries. It underscores a shared commitment to enhancing economic cooperation and promoting free trade despite ongoing global economic challenges.

This trade pact is expected to open new avenues for Vietnam to diversify its export markets and attract high-quality investment, advanced technologies, and modern governance expertise from leading European economies.
Established in 1960, the EFTA is an intergovernmental organisation of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland.
Significant benefits for Norway
Norway stands to gain the most from the agreement. It will ultimately remove tariffs on nearly all goods Norway exports to Vietnam. When the agreement comes into effect, approximately half of Norway’s exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free, with over 98% expected to be tariff-free within seven years, according to a statement from the Norwegian government.

articles.title: Von der Leyen: EU needs whole puzzle of actions for lowering energy prices - Balkan Green Energy News

articles.full_text:
The European Union is rolling out a range of measures against the surge in energy prices, including the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel and extending the temporary state aid framework, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said after the meeting of the European Council. EU leaders are yet to agree on a more comprehensive joint approach to the energy crisis and the tradeoff with carbon pricing. Von der Leyen reiterated the core climate pledges: replacing foreign fossil fuels with affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources and electricity. “We need a whole puzzle of actions,” she pointed out.
The two-day negotiations between EU institutions and member states in Brussels were “long and dense,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged. Speaking alongside European Council President António Costa after their latest summit, she said “there is no silver bullet” for the energy crisis as all countries have different energy mixes.
“We need a whole puzzle of actions,” Von der Leyen pointed out. She noted that since the start of the war in the Middle East, costs for imported fossil fuels have increased by EUR 106 billion, without a single additional molecule of energy. Gas prices have risen 140% since late February, and diesel prices have doubled, Von der Leyen said.
The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves
The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves over the next four months. In addition, it is extending in scope and time the temporary state aid framework introduced in February for vulnerable segments of industrial production. Another recent response with short-term effect was to postpone the Methane Regulation, for monitoring emissions for imported oil and gas, until January 2028.
Von der Leyen noted that the European Commission is opening a strategic dialogue on European refineries, mainly to have more of them operating. Such facilities have been cutting capacity and closing down for years. Their profit margins have substantially narrowed or even gone negative in the past few months. It all translates to a greater dependence on fuel imports.
Transition from imported fossil fuels toward nuclear, renewables is essential
The heads of state and government and top EU executives didn’t find much common ground on the longer-term path forward regarding the tradeoff between climate objectives and expensive energy. For the joint statement, they decided to stick with the core climate pledges from the programs of the previous administration such as REPowerEU, Fit for 55 and the European Green Deal.
“As long as Europe depends on imported oil and gas, our prosperity remains exposed to events beyond our control. This is why it is so important to stay the course of the transition that is a transition towards affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources – nuclear and renewables. We must change the way we consume energy, that is replacing foreign fossil fuels by electricity produced in Europe,” Von der Leyen stressed.
The European Commission’s chief said the grid has to be modernized and improved. Von der Leyen highlighted the 80 GW of renewables capacity installed last year. Six times more is waiting for network connection approval, she asserted.
Member states have specific individual circumstances
The current situation urgently requires a coordinated European response of targeted and temporary measures, taking into account the member states’ specific circumstances and safeguarding the single market, the European Council underlined.
The body welcomed the initiatives of the European Commission to bundle energy demand voluntarily, for joint purchases.
The energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience and structurally lowering energy prices, the European Council said
“Recalling the overarching imperative of reducing the EU’s dependence on volatile fossil fuel markets, the European Council stresses that the energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience, structurally lowering energy prices, and delivering the clean, abundant and homegrown energy needed to power the economy of the future, by accelerating electrification and deploying renewable and low-carbon energy sources, grids and energy storage, as well as fostering energy efficiency,” the conclusions read.
The European Council said the legislative process on the Market Stability Reserve should be accelerated with a view to moderating price volatility. It is a mechanism within the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) designed to fix imbalances between the supply and demand of carbon emission allowances – EUAs. They can be pulled from the market or released back to ease price movements.
In the context of the ongoing review of the ETS system and to support European industrial competitiveness, the European Council repeated that a well-functioning, transparent and predictable carbon market is necessary to effectively protect against carbon leakage, to reduce the volatility of the carbon price and mitigate its impact on electricity prices, while preserving the essential role of the ETS in the climate and energy transition through a market-based price signal for carbon emissions that drives investment and innovation.
The most urgent matter, though, is an agreement on the 27-member bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, needed by the end of this year.
Eurelectric: Beyond short-term response, any measure must be targeted, temporary
In a response to the European Council’s update on energy and climate policy, Eurelectric – Union of the Electricity Industry commended the short-term measures to ease the pressure on bills.
But it pointed out that any further measure must be targeted and temporary, so it does not disrupt the market signals that drive investment.
“Europe must keep its industry competitive while unlocking the investment needed for affordable, secure and decarbonised energy. Eurelectric’s message to leaders is clear: electrification delivers both,” the statement adds. Mirroring the conclusions from the meeting, the association said the energy transition remains the most effective way to lower prices for good and secure Europe’s energy.
There was little word in the European Council about ETS 2 and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Eurelectric said policymakers need to implement ETS 2 rather than reopen it, backed by strong enabling policies and funding instruments like the Social Climate Fund. Early, targeted use of its revenues would protect vulnerable households and give investors certainty, the statement adds.
SolarPower Europe calls for making electrification affordable
SolarPower Europe highlighted the need to ensure a level playing field between electricity and gas. It argued that fairer energy taxation and a strong, predictable carbon price are essential to making electrification the affordable choice.
“Faster deployment of rooftop solar is a proven and swift solution for lowering citizens’ energy bills, while large-scale batteries can store cheap abundant renewable electricity and push out expensive gas peakers when electricity demand is high. These are practical, easy-to-deploy measures that can help shield European households and businesses before next winter,” Deputy Chief Executive Officer Dries Acke said.

Airlines in Europe will have to allow you one personal item - such as a bag - as well as the hand luggage that fits under a seat
Airlines have been told when new regulations will come into force, meaning they have to allow passengers in the EU to take two free bags in hand luggage. The new rules mean anyone flying in the EU must be allowed to take one personal item on board - such as a bag - as well as the hand luggage that has to be found under the seat in front.
The rule was approved by the European Parliament and Council this summer, and dates have now been set for the changes to come into force. A spokesman for the European Parliament said: “The new rules now include the right to carry on board, without additional fee, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack.”
The personal item is in addition to one small bag that must fit under the seat in front of the passenger or be no bigger than 40cm x 30cm x 15cm. The new rules also mean airlines have to advertise prices that include luggage when you start the booking process - not add them later as an 'extra'.
The act has now been signed by the EU Council and Parliament last month and has been published in the EU’s Official Journal. It reads: "Operating air carriers shall, subject to the capacity of the aircraft cabin, permit passengers to carry a piece of hand baggage into the cabin." If the cabin is full, some bags may have to be checked in at no additional cost.
The European Parliament said the changes are expected to come into force from October 23, 2027. It added: “To create price transparency, air fares including allowance for a piece of hand baggage shall be displayed by default before the start of any booking process to facilitate fare comparisons between airlines.
“Negotiators agreed that airlines may offer cheaper tickets for passengers who choose voluntarily to travel without hand luggage.”
It is unclear exactly how flights from the UK will change - as the rules apply in the EU. Rules depend on the departure airport and carrier, not nationality. UK airlines will have to honour the rules on flights departing EU airports, but UK-departing flights could still carry hand luggage charges.
Harry Deacon, travel expert from Holafly, said: "For far too long the rules on hand luggage have been the most aggravating aspect of travel within Europe. One airline on the same route can have a very different allowance from another, and many passengers only discover what they will pay when they reach checkout, or worse still, the airport gate. The inclusion of a free personal item with every flight and the knowledge in advance of what your hand baggage allowance is would go a long way towards making fares more comparable."That all said, I would be wary of sites offering "free cabin luggage" as a synonym for "every bag is free". The personal item is a bit more certain, but the larger cabin bag will still depend on your fare and airline policy and the regulations don't kick in until October 2027. Until then, nothing has changed at the airport. My best advice is to continue to measure your bag against each airline's limits, to carefully check what your fare includes before paying, and to compare the overall price and not the headline fare. And remember that, flying from the UK, you will still be charged on the outbound, even when the return from the EU is free."All in all, this is a major move toward easier-to-understand, more equitable air travel. Passengers should get used to reading fare information now, because they're going to need to do it even more once the new regulation takes effect.”

The agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Vietnam’s top leader To Lam and representatives of the four European countries.
The deal will eliminate or reduce customs duties on a range of goods, including industrial products, fish and agricultural items.
It also covers trade in services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development.
Vietnam’s government said the agreement would help diversify its import and export markets, strengthen its role in global supply chains and support a rules-based trading system amid global economic uncertainty.
Negotiations began in 2012 but stalled in 2018.
The two sides resumed talks in September last year and concluded negotiations in July.
The agreement comes as US tariffs have disrupted global trade and put pressure on Vietnamese exports to the American market.
Experts say closer ties with EFTA economies could help Vietnam broaden its commercial relationships and move towards higher-value manufacturing.
Trade between EFTA and Vietnam reached 4.8 billion euros ($5.4 billion) last year, according to the association.
EFTA’s main exports to Vietnam included electrical and mechanical machinery, fish and pharmaceutical products.
Vietnam mainly exported machinery, footwear and apparel to the four European countries.
EFTA was established as an alternative to the European Economic Community, the predecessor of the European Union.
Its four members maintain close ties with the EU but are not members of the bloc.

Vietnam has signed a free-trade agreement with four European countries, establishing a framework to expand commercial ties and reduce trade barriers between the Southeast Asian economy and members of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA).
The agreement was signed in Hanoi on Sunday by Vietnam and the EFTA members Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein, according to announcements by the Norwegian and Vietnamese governments.
The deal will progressively reduce tariffs on Norwegian exports to Vietnam. Around half of Norway’s exports to the country will be tariff-free when the agreement enters into force, with more than 98 per cent expected to qualify for duty-free access within seven years, the Norwegian government said.
The agreement follows years of negotiations that had remained stalled before being relaunched last year amid growing global tensions over US tariffs. Negotiations concluded in July, paving the way for the formal signing.
The agreement is intended to strengthen commercial relations between Vietnam and the four European countries by improving market access for goods traded between them. Its implementation is expected to provide exporters with a more favourable framework for reaching markets across the two regions.
Vietnam’s trade ministry said the country’s principal exports to EFTA markets include seafood, footwear, textiles, machinery and equipment, electronics and electronic components. Its imports from the four countries mainly comprise industrial machinery and equipment, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and raw materials used in production.
These trade flows reflect the complementary nature of commercial exchanges between Vietnam and the EFTA economies, with Vietnamese exports spanning manufactured goods and consumer products, while imports include industrial inputs and equipment.
Bilateral trade between Vietnam and EFTA member countries has averaged US$2 billion annually, according to Vietnam’s trade ministry. The agreement is intended to provide a basis for expanding those exchanges by reducing trade barriers and improving access to markets.
The tariff reductions outlined by Norway represent a significant element of the deal for Norwegian exporters, although the precise effects across individual industries will depend on the agreement’s implementation and the timetable for removing duties.
The signing also follows the resumption of negotiations last year, when uncertainty surrounding international trade and US tariff policies formed part of the wider context for renewed efforts to conclude the agreement.
With negotiations completed in July and the agreement now signed, Vietnam and the four EFTA countries have established a new framework for their trade relationship. The agreement’s entry into force will determine when the tariff reductions begin to apply and when exporters can start benefiting from the new arrangements.

articles.summary: South Korean Defense Groups Shift to European Production  economy.ac
