South Korean defense groups are moving production into European plants
EU funding rules reward local content, control and design authority
Local lines mature around 2030, as SAFE lending closes
Europe’s military spending increased by 14% in 2025 to $864 billion, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute and some of that demand that would have been hard to predict a decade ago ended up in the Changwon assembly lines. South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration recorded exports of $15.4 billion for the same year, with Poland accounting for more than 40% of the total. South Korean defense groups gained this position because they were delivering tanks and self-propelled guns at a time when European production lines were carrying years of backlogs. The advantage of speed is waning as Brussels ties the new common funds to European content and European control. For Hanwha Aerospace and Hyundai Rotem, the question now shifts to how much industry they are willing to install on European soil and whether their finances will hold up when the current boom in orders weakens.
Readiness 2030, SAFE and EDIP Rewrite the Rules for Non-EU Suppliers
The White Paper on European Defence, known as Readiness 2030, was presented by the European Commission in March 2025 together with the ReArm Europe plan, which aims to mobilise up to €800 billion. Most of this amount comes from the activation of the national escape clause of the Stability and Growth Pact, i.e. from national budgets that gain fiscal space. The second strand is SAFE, a €150 billion loan instrument established by Council Regulation 2025/1106 on 27 May 2025. Poland received the highest allocation, €43.7 billion and Romania the second, €16.68 billion, with the Romanian loan agreement signed on May 12, 2026, i.e. these are the two markets where Korean companies have invested the most. The third tool is the European Defence Industry Programme, the EDIP, established by Regulation 2025/2643 in December 2025 with a budget of €1.5 billion, of which over €700 million is directed, according to the work programme adopted by the Commission on 30 March 2026, to increasing European production.
Article 16 of SAFE stipulates that contractors and subcontractors must be established in the Union, in an EEA EFTA State or in Ukraine, have their executive management there and not be controlled by a third country, with the possibility of derogation where the entity has passed a foreign direct investment screening or when the State of establishment confirms security guarantees. The often misinterpreted threshold of 35% does not refer to the contract value. It measures the cost of components sourced from outside the eligible territories as a percentage of the estimated cost of the final product components, which makes the origin of the fire control system or power unit much more important than the place of final assembly. The regulation allows bilateral agreements with countries that have a Security and Defence Partnership with the Union and Canada became the first non-European country to secure such an agreement, with Member States’ endorsement in December 2025. South Korea signed its own Partnership in November 2024, however the EU-Korea summit in Brussels in June 2026 resulted in the opening of negotiations on a classified information security agreement rather than participation in SAFE.
The EDIP also explicitly sets out a design authority requirement. Beyond the corresponding 35% threshold in Article 10, the beneficiary must be able to modify the product and replace components throughout its lifecycle without a third-country veto, with the possibility of a legally binding commitment to full autonomy by 31 December 2033. National procurement with national funds is left out of both regimes, so the image of a Europe that collectively excludes Korean weapons is inaccurate. A K9 that Warsaw buys with its own money is not judged by the rules of SAFE, while the same K9, if financed by a SAFE loan, must pass the criteria of origin and control and if it claims support from the EDIP it must also prove that Seoul does not hold a key in its design. The three channels are not interchangeable and this explains why local production has become a matter of access to specific sources of financing for Korean groups.
Hanwha Aerospace Moves Production to Romania and Poland
Romania signed a contract with Hanwha Aerospace in July 2024 for 54 K9 self-propelled guns and 36 K10 ammunition resupply vehicles, thus becoming the sixth NATO member state to use the K9. Nineteen months later, on February 12, 2026, the subsidiary Hanwha Aerospace Romania, founded in 2025 as a Romanian company, laid the foundation stone of the Hanwha Armoured Vehicle Centre of Excellence Europe in Petrești, Dâmbovița County. The facility will cover approximately 181,055 square meters, with assembly lines, test facilities, a 1,751-meter driving track and research and development laboratories. The company presents it as its first production base in Europe, initially focused on assembly, integration, testing, and lifecycle support for the K9 and K10, to localize up to 80% through Romanian industry. According to the company, cooperation with more than 30 Romanian partners has already begun.
In Poland the format is different. On September 3, 2025, the first day of the MSPO exhibition in Kielce, Hanwha Aerospace and the Polish group WB Group signed an agreement for a joint venture that will locally produce the CGR-080 guided missile, with a range of about 80 kilometers, for the Polish army’s Homar-K multiple launcher system. The agreement provides for a gradual transfer of technology, about 250 positions of specialized personnel and serial production that will reach an advanced stage before the end of 2028. Four months later, on December 29, 2025, the Polish Armaments Agency signed an executive contract worth about 14 billion zlotys, close to $4 billion, with a consortium led by the Hanwha WB Advanced System joint venture. The missiles will be manufactured in a special unit within Poland and deliveries will begin in 2030.
The two schemes share a logic that goes beyond assembly. Ammunition is being consumed and a guided missile factory in Poland is securing revenue for as long as the Polish military is training and replenishing stockpiles, while a lifecycle center in Romania is turning maintenance, upgrades and spare parts into local infrastructure, which a competitor would struggle to displace after a decade of operation with Romanian personnel and Romanian suppliers. One detail in the text of the Polish agreement stands out, as the roadmap for new types of missiles will be drafted in accordance with both Polish defense procurement rules and the Republic of Korea’s export control regime. The joint venture has a Polish base and a Polish co-owner; the relevant announcements did not disclose each side's percentage of participation and the technology transfer continues to follow licenses issued in Seoul.
Hyundai Rotem’s K2PL Localizes Assembly but Keeps Design Control in Korea
Hyundai Rotem took a different route in the same country. The framework agreement approved in Warsaw on July 27, 2022 concerns a total of 1,000 K2 tanks and their Polonised version, the K2PL, along with support vehicles, training and technology transfer. The first executive contract of August 2022, with a net value of $3.37 billion, covered 180 K2 tanks made in Korea and the last batch of 20 tanks arrived in Poland on November 13, 2025. The second contract, signed on August 1, 2025 at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice, is valued at around $6.5 billion and provides for another 180 tanks. Of these, 116 in the K2GF configuration are delivered from 2026 to 2027 and 64 in the K2PL configuration from 2028 to 2030, with the first three K2PLs being built in Korea for testing and the remaining 61 in Gliwice. The contract also includes 31 armoured recovery vehicles, 25 engineering vehicles and 25 bridge-laying vehicles, with delivery from 2029 to 2031.
The technology transfer outlined by the Polish Ministry of National Defense for the second contract is specific and delimited: the possibility of final assembly in Polish companies and the ability to fully maintain and operate the tanks. Hyundai Rotem undertakes to equip Bumar-Łabędy with tools and machinery for the K2PL line and the accompanying vehicles. On April 27, 2026, the two companies signed the agreement regulating production, with Bumar-Łabędy assembling 61 K2PL tanks and 72 support vehicles as a subcontractor, while Hyundai Rotem remains the main contractor of the program and with the first K2PL coming off the Gliwice line in 2028. In relation to the K2GF, the K2PL acquires an active vehicle protection system, a drone-countering system and additional armor, while it will be able to use programmable ammunition of other origins and a Polish 12.7mm heavy machine gun.
The comparison with Hanwha Aerospace is mainly about who raises the capital and who holds the control. Hanwha Aerospace invests in its own European entities, a Romanian subsidiary and a Polish joint venture, taking on the risk of facilities that need to be filled with orders. Hyundai Rotem installs a line in a Polish state-owned company of the PGZ group and retains the position of main contractor and designer, with much less exposure to fixed assets. The second model fits more easily into the establishment and control criterion of Article 16, since the manufacturer is Polish, but leaves open the origin of the components and the design authority, which remain largely Korean. The leadership of the Polish Ministry of National Defense has stated that it wants K2PL to become an export success for Łabędy, an ambition that presupposes an agreement on who has the right to sell to third parties a tank designed in Korea and assembled in Silesia.

Investing.com -- European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde urged governments to maintain sustainable public finances, warning that rising debt and energy-related inflation risks threaten economic stability.
Speaking at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings in Thailand, Lagarde described fiscal sustainability as a crucial foundation for broader economic stability.
She called on governments to adhere to fiscal rules, reduce excessive debt and improve public spending efficiency to rebuild financial buffers.
Lagarde also urged policymakers to ensure that measures addressing the ongoing energy shock remain temporary and targeted, rather than creating additional long-term fiscal pressures.
Her remarks followed discussions among global finance ministers and central bankers about mounting public debt, geopolitical tensions and the economic implications of artificial intelligence.
Lagarde emphasised that restoring an international economic framework based on openness, predictability and established rules would support global trade and investment.
ECB Governing Council member Olli Rehn echoed those concerns, stressing the importance of international cooperation amid increasing economic fragmentation.
Turning to the eurozone, Lagarde reiterated the ECB's assessment that economic growth faces downside risks, while inflation risks remain tilted upward.
She warned that the energy shock was too significant to disregard, although a measured monetary policy response remained appropriate.
The ECB has raised interest rates twice this year, in June and September, as policymakers seek to contain inflationary pressures.
Markets widely expect another increase before year-end, reflecting concerns that elevated energy costs could keep inflation above the central bank's target.
ECB Governing Council member Joachim Nagel suggested further monetary tightening might be necessary, while supporting the bank's meeting-by-meeting approach.
Rehn said monetary policy would continue prioritising price stability to support sustainable economic growth.
Lagarde also revealed that more than 30 central banks had expressed interest in the Eurosystem's enhanced repurchase agreement facility, designed to support monetary policy transmission and strengthen the euro's international role.

Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.
The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".
Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.
"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.
Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.
More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.
Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."
The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".
eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

articles.summary: From Banking to Taxis, Ukraine’s Data Center Strikes Disrupt Everyday Life in Russia  The Moscow TimesRussians Lose Access To Homes, Bank Accounts After Ukraine Hits Data Centres  NDTVIs Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?  BBCUkraine’s drone strikes on Russian data centres may change how we see disinformation  The ConversationDid Ukraine's data center strikes affect Russia's bot army? articles.full_text:
Andrei, a 39-year-old journalist from Moscow, looks at the notification on his smartphone and laughs.
“Damn! I can’t log into my Yandex Pay account, but they’re still charging me for a Yandex Music subscription that doesn’t even work,” he says.
When he tried to log in, the app displayed a message that said “Something went wrong” and asked him to try again later.
“It’s a good thing I use another bank’s card for most of my payments,” he says.
Yandex Pay is one of dozens of services whose operations have been disrupted by Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers this month.
For many Russians, these outages have mostly meant temporary inconveniences and changes to their routines. But in a year that has already seen widespread fuel shortages, airport closures and e-commerce disruptions due to the war, they are the latest way in which the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has seeped into everyday life.
The data-center strikes have disrupted everything from taxis and car-sharing services, food delivery and maps to email, banking and streaming platforms.
Problems also arose for state agencies and private firms whose products rely on Yandex infrastructure, from dating apps to access systems for residential complexes and smart homes.
‘Far more serious than we expected’
Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30% of normal levels following the Oct. 8-11 strikes, according to internet monitoring group NetBlocks. The disruptions affected 84 cloud services.
Yandex confirmed serious damage to one data center, the shutdown of another and infrastructure disruptions at a third. It has not disclosed the full extent of the damage or given a timeline for recovery.
In addition, all three of Yandex’s supercomputers were likely severely affected, which could set Russia back years in the AI race, the science news outlet T-Invariant said.
After a further strike hit a VK data center in St. Petersburg on Sunday, users also reported disruptions on social network VKontakte, including photos failing to load.
As of Monday, Yandex Pay remained only partially available. The error message had been replaced with a reassurance: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”
The Moscow Times reporter who wrote this article was still unable to access their full Yandex Taxi ride history on Monday.
A senior data analyst at Yandex told The Moscow Times that the company had been preparing for data center outages even before this month’s strikes.
“But the scale turned out to be far more serious than we initially expected,” and Yandex’s rank-and-file employees were caught off guard, said the employee, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal matters.
“We had to drop everything and focus on urgent problems with our services,” he said. “We managed to mitigate some of the effects quickly by switching applications to limited functionality, while in other cases recovery took several days.”
He said it could take much longer to fully restore services.
“I don’t think anyone expects everything to be fully restored within a few days,” the employee said.
The analyst declined to discuss how Yandex was preparing for further Ukrainian strikes, saying that disclosing those plans could create a vulnerability for the company.
From bank accounts to court hearings
While the economic damage and longer-term consequences of the strikes remain unclear, the immediate disruption has been manageable for many users.
The names of private individuals interviewed for this article have been changed for their safety.
Robert, a barista in St. Petersburg, uses Yandex Pay as his main bank account. It’s where he receives his salary and other transfers.
“I use it for payments 99% of the time,” he said. “Luckily, I had almost no money in my account when the outage happened. I’d spent everything on big purchases shortly beforehand. So I wasn’t too worried about losing it forever.”
His access to his digital wallet was restored after several days. Hee said he has no plans to stop using Yandex.
“I always keep an alternative way to pay just in case — a little cash,” he said.
The attack has nevertheless made him think about the war.
“It’s another reminder that the consequences of the war are getting closer to home — and growing in scale,” he said.
The disruptions also reached Yandex users outside Russia.
Yekaterina, a Russian woman who moved to Georgia after the invasion of Ukraine, said Yandex Go, a taxi service widely used across former Soviet countries, was temporarily unavailable in Tbilisi.
Nikolai, a Russian doctoral student in New Zealand, said he was unable to use Yandex Archives to research his dissertation.
“There weren’t many sources there, but the search was really convenient. So I sat down to write a chapter, wanted to quote something, and the archive was gone!” he said.
The data center strikes have also affected government agencies. The exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported that dozens of court hearings across Russia were disrupted due to technical problems.
Some government websites in the Kaluga region also went offline, Sarkis Darbinyan, an IT lawyer and founder of digital rights organization RKS.global, told The Moscow Times.
The outages have posed particular problems for small and medium-sized businesses whose products run on Yandex’s infrastructure, especially its cloud platform, a Russian equivalent of Google Cloud.
Tatyana, the founder of fitness app FIT&ZEN, told customers that both the app and its web version were temporarily unavailable because of “technical problems at a Yandex data center.”
“A major Yandex outage has affected many companies across the country, so unfortunately we’re not alone in this,” she wrote on the company’s Telegram channel.
A strike on Yandex Cloud hits “thousands of Russian companies at once,” Darbinyan said.
“After the Kremlin pushed Google and all its cloud competitors out of the country, Yandex played a very important role in the Russian internet, even though it did not have a dominant share of the data center market,” he said.
The greatest risks face customers that cut costs by keeping all their data in a single availability zone without backups elsewhere, he added. These include small and medium-sized businesses, regional media outlets and government agencies.
Can Ukraine knock Russia’s internet offline?
Darbinyan said the vulnerabilities exposed by the strikes are rooted partly in the structure of Russia’s internet and the rules governing where companies can store their data.
Earlier this month, the operator of Ukraine’s Parkovyi data center moved copies of customers’ data to backup sites in the European Union after it was hit by Russian strikes.
By comparison, Russian companies have little scope to do the same, Darbinyan said. Data localization laws and rules governing hosting, authentication services and critical information infrastructure require them to store data inside Russia.
Even so, Darbinyan said it would be difficult to take Russia’s internet completely offline by striking data centers.
Despite the Kremlin’s efforts to isolate it through its “sovereign internet” policy, Russia’s internet remains a vast network built along the same lines as the global internet. It encompasses more than 200 data centers, hundreds of telecom network nodes and corporate server rooms.
Its greatest vulnerability is the concentration of commercial data center capacity in Moscow and nearby regions, with much of it owned by a handful of major companies: Yandex, VK, Rostelecom and Sberbank, he said.
Serious disruptions at those companies can therefore affect services nationwide.
Nor will it be easy or quick to replace damaged infrastructure. Russia obtains almost all the necessary equipment through parallel imports, while the AI boom has driven up prices, Darbinyan said.
“If strikes become regular, the market may simply not be able to keep up with replacing what’s been lost,” he said.

articles.title: Vietnam-EU trade relations face new developments. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam-EU trade relations face new developments.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The latest figures show that Vietnam-EU economic relations are at their most vibrant stage since the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) came into effect.
Bilateral trade has increased at double-digit rates. Vietnam's trade surplus continues to expand. Belgium, Europe's logistics gateway, has emerged as a potentially untapped partner. However, behind these impressive figures lie increasingly stringent EU market demands and the growing pressure to balance trade.
According to data from the European Statistical Agency (Eurostat), published by the Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security of the European Commission in May 2026, the EU imported €63.9 billion worth of goods from Vietnam in 2025, a 16% increase compared to the previous year. Vietnam became the bloc's ninth largest supplier, surpassing Japan , and accounted for 2.5% of total imports from outside the EU. Total bilateral trade reached €76 billion, an increase of approximately 67% compared to 2019, before the EVFTA came into effect.
Several Vietnamese products have become irreplaceable in this market. Machinery and electrical equipment account for more than half of the EU's imports from Vietnam, reaching 33.8 billion euros. In telecommunications equipment alone, Vietnam supplies nearly 15% of the EU's total imports from outside the bloc. Even more noteworthy, one in four pairs of footwear imported by the EU comes from Vietnam. Agricultural products have also seen strong growth, with plant-based products such as coffee, cashews, and pepper reaching 4.5 billion euros, an increase of over 40% in just one year.
The growth trend is expected to continue in 2026. According to the Vietnam Trade Office in Belgium and the EU, citing EU statistics, bilateral trade reached €52.6 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 23.2% increase compared to the same period last year. Of this, Vietnam exported €45.6 billion, a 26% increase, and imported €7 billion, a 6% increase. Data released by the General Statistics Office ( Ministry of Finance ) on October 3rd also shows that in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam had a trade surplus with the EU of US$36.06 billion, a 25.3% increase. This figure is even more significant considering that the country's overall trade balance has shifted to a deficit of US$19.42 billion.
The political foundation for these figures has just been elevated to a new level. In January 2026, during the visit of the President of the European Council, Antonio Costa, to Vietnam, the two sides upgraded their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. In Hanoi, Mr. Costa emphasized that "this is the EU's first Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in Southeast Asia." Regarding the economic pillar, the EU is currently Vietnam's fourth largest trading partner and sixth largest investor, while Vietnam is the EU's largest trading partner in ASEAN.
You may also like
The EVFTA has also just reached an important milestone. According to the European Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam (EuroCham), from the seventh year of implementation (August 2026), the EU will complete its tariff reduction roadmap, meaning 99% of Vietnamese exports will be tariff-free when entering the EU market. Vietnam will continue to reduce tariffs on EU goods until 2030. As EuroCham President Bruno Jaspaert put it, "Six years ago, it was an ambitious political commitment. Today, its impact is measurable."
In its relationship with the EU, Belgium holds a special position. It is not only home to EU institutions but also a logistics hub with the port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe's largest cargo gateways. By 2025, Vietnam-Belgium trade is projected to reach US$4.36 billion. In the first eight months of 2026, this figure has already exceeded US$3 billion, with Vietnam exporting approximately US$2.7 billion. Belgium is Vietnam's sixth largest trading partner in the EU, while Vietnam is Belgium's largest trading partner in ASEAN. By the end of 2025, Belgium had 104 investment projects in Vietnam with a total capital of over US$1.1 billion. Compared to Belgium's economic scale and standing, these figures demonstrate significant potential for further cooperation.
In an interview with a Vietnam News Agency (VNA) reporter in Brussels, the Vietnamese Ambassador to Belgium and Head of the Vietnamese Delegation to the EU, Nguyen Huong Tra, stated: "After more than half a century of developing relations, it is time for both sides to explore new areas of cooperation, in which science and technology and training high-quality human resources are areas where Belgium has strengths and Vietnam has great needs." According to the Ambassador, cooperation in logistics, seaports, and strategic infrastructure promises to create a ripple effect for both countries. Building on the Strategic Partnership on Agriculture established in 2018, both sides can further expand into green agriculture and smart agriculture.
However, the trade picture isn't all rosy. According to Eurostat data, while imports from Vietnam are projected to increase by 16%, EU exports to Vietnam are expected to decline slightly by 1% in 2025, to €12.2 billion. Consequently, the EU's trade deficit with Vietnam is projected to increase from €42.7 billion to €51.7 billion in just one year. Vietnam ranks only 30th among EU export markets. This widening gap is likely to become a topic of discussion in bilateral dialogue.
European businesses have chosen a more conciliatory approach. "Although Vietnam maintains a large trade surplus with the EU, this shouldn't be viewed in a win-lose mindset," commented Jean-Jacques Bouflet, Vice President of EuroCham and former head of the EU's EVFTA negotiating team. According to him, the EU currently accounts for about 12% of Vietnam's exports but only 4% of its imports. Increasing imports of high-quality technology, machinery, and pharmaceuticals from Europe would both help balance trade and enhance the long-term competitiveness of Vietnam's industry.
The second challenge stems from regulatory barriers. The Vietnamese Trade Office in Belgium and the EU has warned businesses to proactively adapt to a series of new EU regulations on environment, packaging, e-commerce, and traceability, especially in the steel, agricultural, and food sectors. Mr. Bouflet also stated that the ability to meet the requirements of the European Green Deal, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and the European Union Forest Regulation (EUDR) will increasingly become a decisive factor in competitiveness.
You may also like
Some old bottlenecks remain unresolved. The IUU (Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated) fishing "yellow card" against Vietnamese seafood is still in effect after nearly 10 years. Ambassador Guerrier acknowledged that lifting it is not yet possible, but affirmed that both sides "are on the right track." The Vietnam-EU Investment Protection Agreement (EVIPA) is still awaiting ratification by all member states. According to EuroCham, this is a "strategic priority" to allow European capital, which grows much slower than trade, to flow strongly into clean energy, digital infrastructure, and high-tech manufacturing sectors.
Vietnam's first-mover advantage is also narrowing. Ambassador Guerrier stated that, at the same time as upgrading relations with Vietnam, the EU has finalized free trade agreements with the Southern Common Market (Mercosur) and India, and more recently with the Philippines and Indonesia, while also negotiating with Malaysia and Thailand. Vietnam will no longer be the only ASEAN country with preferential access to a market of nearly 450 million people.
In the context of the EU's push to diversify its supply chains, Vietnam has a great opportunity to become a reliable link for Europe in Asia. However, this opportunity will only materialize when trade develops more harmoniously, when Vietnamese businesses meet the highest standards, and when investment capital keeps pace with the flow of goods. Therefore, the visit of General Secretary and President To Lam not only strengthens political trust, but also provides an opportunity for both sides to translate high-level commitments into concrete projects, orders, and capital flows, as Ambassador Nguyen Huong Tra emphasized: political will alone is not enough; the involvement of businesses, localities, and people from both sides is necessary.

Rising bond yields worldwide in recent weeks have reflected concerns about government debt, persistent inflation and increased competition for credit from investments in artificial intelligence. France, which carries a heavy debt burden, has been among the countries most affected by the selloff.

According to Reuters, Lagarde said tighter financing conditions would slow economic activity and reduce the extent to which higher energy prices linked to the Iran war feed through to broader inflation, although the impact could differ from the ECB's previous projections.
Speaking at a gathering of central bankers and finance ministers in Bangkok, Lagarde said long-term interest rates had risen notably since the central bank's previous policy meeting, making financial conditions tighter than anticipated.

However, policymakers remain concerned that higher energy costs could spread to other prices and wages, making inflation more persistent.
Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel indicated that further monetary tightening could be necessary, while stressing that decisions would depend on incoming economic data at each meeting. He said the ECB's fight against inflation was not yet complete and that additional action might be required.
ECB policymaker Olli Rehn, Finland's central bank governor, said the bank would closely monitor potential second-round effects from energy inflation. Such effects occur when higher energy costs lead to broader price increases and wage demands, potentially creating a more persistent inflation cycle.
Rehn noted that there were no signs of such effects so far but said the ECB would remain vigilant.
The latest bond market turmoil presents a challenge for the ECB as it seeks to contain inflation without placing excessive pressure on an economy already facing higher energy costs and tighter financing conditions. Policymakers will continue to assess incoming data to determine whether further interest rate increases are needed.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, a think tank, says the Chancellor faces a £35bn hole in his maiden Budget, which means without cutting benefits he could be forced to raise taxes.
But the Chancellor has limited room for manoeuvre. Labour was elected on a manifesto that promised not to raise income tax, National Insurance or VAT.
Ahead of the Budget, Healey was reportedly looking at cutting the “mansion tax” threshold from £2m to £1.5m and aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates – but he has since ruled out both measures.
Nevertheless, previous Labour budgets have left savers worried about further tax rises for wealthy savers.
So far, the Government has brought pensions into the inheritance tax net and increased tax rates on savings income and rental income from 2027.
Harrison says: “They’re coming after all the other sources of wealth, and I think [the tax-free lump sum] would be an easy one to pick.”
The over-55s can withdraw 25pc of their pension pot tax-free, up to a maximum of £268,275. In 2024-25 and 2025-26, savers pulled out £40bn in tax-free cash – more than the total withdrawn in the previous five-year period – amid fears Labour could introduce a cap.
This year, however, there have not been any specific rumours that Healey is considering this move, and the investment platform AJ Bell has urged the Government to leave pensions untouched in the Budget so as not to discourage saving.
Harrison says he’s concerned about the impact of today’s high-tax environment on young workers. He recently stepped away from permanent roles in the financial services industry to go freelance – partly for greater flexibility, but also because he’s tired of “paying almost 50pc tax”.
Income tax thresholds have been frozen until 2031, dragging millions into higher tax bands.
“It feels like the message is there’s no point in building wealth, because it’s just going to get taxed,” he says.
